Set against the backdrop of 1860s Kyoto—a time of crumbling empires, brewing revolution, and supernatural secrets—Hakuoki: Kyoto Winds is an otome visual novel that mixes historical fiction, political intrigue, and tragic romance with elegant storytelling. Originally released as part of the Hakuoki series and later reimagined for the PS Vita and PC, this version is both a solid entry point for newcomers and a rewarding expansion for returning fans.

You play as Chizuru Yukimura, a young woman searching for her missing father in a politically unstable Kyoto. Along the way, she crosses paths with the Shinsengumi, the infamous samurai police force loyal to the shogunate. But all is not as it seems—beneath the rigid honor and discipline lies a darker truth involving secret experiments, hidden pasts, and the supernatural.

Yes, this is a romance game—but it's also a war story. A slow-burn drama about loyalty, sacrifice, and personal identity in a world on the brink of collapse.

Kyoto Winds introduces a whopping 13 potential love interests, each with unique personalities, routes, and endings. Some are stoic and principled (like Hijikata), others are warm and protective (like Okita), and a few are wildcards, including newcomers not present in earlier Hakuoki entries.

Every route branches early and often, with meaningful choices that affect not only your romantic outcome but also who lives, who dies, and how much of the game’s deep lore you uncover. The emotional payoff is often gutting—don’t expect sunshine and rainbows. Expect to suffer beautifully.

What Hakuoki does so well is tone. The writing is mature, atmospheric, and drenched in a sense of historical melancholy. It’s not just about choosing a romantic partner—it’s about watching people you care about wrestle with duty, mortality, and fading ideals.

The romance feels earned, not rushed. Chizuru is more than a passive observer—she grows, learns, and stands up for herself, even if she’s not a sword-wielding heroine.

The game doesn’t shy away from tragedy either. Many routes reflect the grim fate of the Shinsengumi in history, lending weight to even the tenderest moments.

Visually, Kyoto Winds is stunning. Character art is elegant, with detailed kimono designs, expressive portraits, and beautiful backdrops of Edo-period Japan. Every moment—be it a quiet snowfall or a heated sword clash—feels drenched in mood.

The soundtrack matches perfectly: subtle, traditional, and often tinged with sadness. It doesn’t overwhelm but enhances, especially during emotional turning points.

As a visual novel, gameplay is limited to choices, but Kyoto Winds offers plenty of quality-of-life features: fast-forward, auto-text, a flowchart to track choices, and multiple save slots. That said, the pacing can be slow, especially in the common route (shared across multiple characters), and newcomers may feel overwhelmed by the historical detail or sheer number of branching paths.

Also important: this is only Part 1 of a larger story. It ends many routes on cliffhangers that resolve in Hakuoki: Edo Blossoms, so be ready for a two-part commitment.

Hakuoki: Kyoto Winds is a haunting, emotionally rich visual novel that goes far beyond romance. With layered characters, beautiful writing, and a strong historical setting tinged with fantasy, it’s a standout in the otome genre. If you’re looking for swoon-worthy samurai with tragic pasts, quiet yearning, and poetic goodbyes, this game delivers in spades.

A slow-burning, beautifully drawn saga of love and loss—just make sure you’re ready for heartbreak.

[h1]Hakuoki: Kyoto Winds – A Captivating Historical Fantasy[/h1]
Hakuoki: Kyoto Winds is a beautifully crafted visual novel that immerses players in the turbulent Bakumatsu period of Japan, blending historical intrigue with supernatural romance. As Chizuru Yukimura, a determined young woman searching for her missing father, players navigate the complex world of the Shinsengumi—a group of elite samurai with dark secrets.

[b]Engaging Story & Rich Characters[/b]
The narrative is a masterful mix of historical drama and fantasy, offering a fresh perspective on the famed Shinsengumi. The writing is immersive, pulling players into the political conflicts, personal struggles, and hidden mysteries of Kyoto. The 12 romanceable bachelors—including six new additions—each bring depth and unique personalities, ensuring varied and emotionally compelling routes.

[b]Visual & Audio Excellence[/b]
The remastered visuals breathe life into the game, with fluid animations and vibrant artwork that enhance the historical setting. The character designs are striking, and the CGs are beautifully detailed. The Japanese voice acting is superb, adding authenticity, while the soundtrack complements the emotional and action-packed moments perfectly.

[b]Player Choice & Replayability[/b]
With over 30 endings, Kyoto Winds rewards exploration. Choices matter, subtly shaping relationships and leading to vastly different outcomes. While some paths require careful navigation, the branching narratives ensure high replay value. The inclusion of a "Record of Service" feature allows players to revisit key moments, making completionist runs more manageable.

[b]A Few Minor Quibbles[/b]
As the first part of a two-game series, Kyoto Winds ends on a cliffhanger, leaving some storylines unresolved until Edo Blossoms. Additionally, the pacing can feel slow in the early chapters, but the payoff is worth it as the tension escalates.

[b]Final Verdict[/b]
Hakuoki: Kyoto Winds is a must-play for visual novel enthusiasts, especially those who enjoy historical settings with a supernatural twist. Its compelling storytelling, stunning visuals, and memorable characters make it a standout title. Whether you're a longtime fan or new to the series, this remastered journey through Kyoto is an unforgettable experience.

Note that this is a review for both halves of the game, Kyoto Winds and Edo Blossoms. 

I’m changing my review again because this game has temporarily consumed my life. 

So first of all, I got the worst start on this game which explained my initial lukewarm reaction. Do not make my mistake, do not watch the anime. The anime is an absolute trainwreck and only really there for fans who are already invested. 

Also don’t play Hijikata’s route first. It’s often considered the ‘main’ story route, but there are a few problems with it.
The first being as an introduction to the game, it doesn’t let Chizuru get in the thick of things. She doesn’t bond with the other Shinsengumi and it makes the game feel like it’s listing historical events one after the other, just tugging you along without leaving much of an impact.

Because you don’t bond with the other Shinsengumi, you don’t feel the weight of Hijikata’s story. His is a story about the burden of leadership and what happens to such a man when he’s on the losing side of history.
I still have a lot of complaints about his route, because I never got the sense he was really growing close to Chizuru. He’s quite cold and dismissive of her really late into the second half of the game, which makes his eventual confession feel a bit out of the blue. 

But there's so many routes in this game I'm sure you'll find one you love.

The art is of course gorgeous, the music is fantastic and I can’t get the opening songs out of my head. 

There are so many possible routes in this game it’s a bit overwhelming. It’s also quite a time sink, unlike a lot of indie visual novels all the main routes at least seem to be vastly different stories and you only get a fraction of the bigger picture each time. You can’t play this game once and have closure, you have to keep going. 

This could be good or bad depending on how you like your romance routes. 

There is a lot of sexism in this game depending on the romance option you pick. Harada is quite sweet and for the most part quite respectful aside from the usual 'men should protect women' stuff. 
There are a few moments that are entirely inventions of the subtitles. 'This isn't for a lady's eyes' was a translation of 'you shouldn't see this.' Hijikata's language in particular is made harsher by the translation. 
Harada also calls Chizuru 'kid' in the subtitles. Rest assured he's calling her nothing of the sort. He calls Chizuru by her name or just 'omae' which is a rough form of 'you.'

The dialogue subtitles are a bit nuts, and considering my Japanese is pretty bad it's a bit concerning that I've noticed it. But that's not the fault of the game.The actual writing translation is really good!

And of course, the voice acting is top notch. You'll recognise quite a few famous voices if you're an anime fan - though it is Japanese only.

I'm not finished with the game, so I'll update it later, but here's my review so far--if you want to read something this in-depth.

[b]Gameplay:[/b] Definitely not your typical otome game. There are a lot of politics--none that you really HAVE to keep up with, but it helps understand the storyline--and lots of action. Which I love. I thought at first it was strictly historical fiction/romance, as it takes place in 1860s, but you quickly learn that there is a strong streak of fantasy/paranormal [spoiler] including demons and scientific experiments [/spoiler], which is very fun. Hakuoki: Kyoto Winds is part one of a two part remake of the classic Hakuoki: Demon of the Fleeting Blossom dating sim. PROS
-12 Unique, likable bachelors with engaging, individual plotlines
-Gorgeous and consistent art
-Stunning soundtrack
-Excellent writing
-Tons of replay value

CONS
-Only half the story, to be continued in Hakuoki: Edo Blossoms
-An utterly massive amount of information overload regarding 1860s Japanese government systems. Truly, far too much information. If you're a real big historical fiction fan or history buff in general, you are in for a treat. Otherwise, buckle up, kiddo.
-Awkward user interface. Sometimes feels like a lazy PS Vita port.

If you're a fan of the original game, Hakuoki: Kyoto Winds is worth picking up for the new content. If you're a new player, and a fan of dating sims, it's a must play.

This game makes me so happy. The original game meant so much to me and was a great inspiration for my current hobbies, like drawing and writing. Seeing a remaster of it and then learning I can play it on my PC a few days afterwards made me feel so happy. I'm a little sad that I do not meet one of the requirements of signing up for being a beta tester for part 2 and that by the time I found out it was halfway through the sign ups already, but knowing that it is comeing out soon is making me look foreward to it with excitement and is also giving me a reason to save up my money.

The Actual game itself is great. Compared to the original that I played almost four years ago it is much better. The Dialouge is more fleshed out to dive deeper into the personalities of the characters and makes them even more "human" so to speak. This also includes the MC (Chizuru) who in the original I found to be a bit plain and would not seem like such a good character if not for you being able to read her thoughts through the narrative. However in this she makes a lot more actions and her speach gives her much more personality as well, which makes me appreciate the character. Side stories in Demon of the Fleeting Blossom are now added into the story so you don't have to save and exit to the main screen to read it in what you can guess to be the correct ordor. I am a bit sad that the "Shinsengumi Adventures" 1 and 2 were not added in, but it does make replaying the old version for it both worth it, yet also kind of tedious since it means I have to set up my old gameing console up again, but those are first world problems (but since I have a weak will and am basically addicted to these kinds of games I would not be apposed to buying a future DLC containing these two side stories and perphaps some extras. Just saying, Game Devs *wink wink*)
As for the new design outside of the writing I am also impressed. The new soundtrack completely replaces the old and I know there is a debate on which is better but I believe that the soundtrack in this fits better with the time of the readers and makes it easier to emerse myself into the emotion of what is going on whether it be a calm, tension, anger, joy, or even a bit of melencholy. Both soundtracks are great, however, and it depends on what I feel, personally. The newly updated designs of existing characters in the form of clothes is good too. It makes them higher quality and also makes them seem a lot more fancy and stand out more compared to the old ones. However, having said this, there are some characters I believe had a better fashion sense in the old games. For example: I believe Souji Okita's red Kimono looked better with the rings and over a black undershirt instead of a green with a golden rim, and the white pants just pop out too much while his old green ones blended nicely with the red shirt. The Blue undershirt and sleaves on Heisuke Toudou throw me off a bit since I remember them being a purple and they are similar, yet side by side I prefer the purple. I also think that Sanosuke Harada's old vest had a more astheticlly appealing design in my opinion. But just as there are some I thought looked better before there are those that I think are better now. Like Shinpachi Nagakura. When I first saw him in black instead of his old green scheme I was confused, yet it quickly grew on me.
There is also the mention of smaller details like background blurs, blood being added to models when they are injured, snow, leaves, and blossoms falling down the screen when a certain weather is described or hinted at, the quick splatters of blood across the screen, and the shifting of frame to show a change in possition in certain scenes (like in the prologue when Chizuru peaks from behind the stacked boards) were all great and helped me feel even more immersed.

Now comes the new characters. I think it is good to have new characters added in to allow for old fans, like myself and many others here, to have new experiences in the form of memorable side characters now being romanceable or even fully new ones to give us even more characters to love. However it does seem like they were just plopped in since outside of their routes they only appear once each (with the exception of Ryouma Sakamoto who will only appear when your trying to go down his or Hajime Saito's Route.) Sure, adding them in outside of their routes more could change the story and even make it longer which I understand some just do not have that kind of time, but would help make one feel closer to them outside of the route and even make them want to do it not just for the "He's new, I'mma check him out and see what's up" or "Hot diggidy dog, I'm comeing for that precious booty" cause that only goes so far.

So those were my thoughts on the game, and I hope this is enough information to give to those looking to buy it for a deeper look into it to help them see what is in store yet not too much cause spoilers are punishable by death where I'm from. Also if there is a small chance that the creators of this game will see it (but I doubt it) I hope this helped them understand how much I enjoy these games and that I am going to support them with the series by buying their games.

Kyoto Winds is more slice of life than a dating sim, with a darker setting. If you are a fan of post-apocalyptic this is a great title for you. You have cast of 12 male characters with most of the stories having overlap since it mostly takes place at the Kyoto Head quarters of the Shinsengumi. You visit locations and more "hangout" with the Routes interest. Each is managing to stand out so far. Currently Hijikata (Edo only) -> Okita -> Harada -> Yamazaki -> Saito -> Ida -> Toudou. Harada is probably the least complicated (in a good way) making him in my opinion the Best Husbando material and Yamazaki was a dark horse.  After playing Toudou I ship him and the MC as the cannon romance since they instantly hit it off. 

All 12 LI have left an impression on me. I am least looking forward to Sanan and Nagagura. Where the cast succeeds is the fact they are all grown men and it is alluded to most of them engage in philandering. Primarily the cast is singly focused on the conflict around them and their duty. However you do get to see many sides as you witness their friendships as well their more serious sides. There is a lot of bickering between the cast which is great. The interaction with the MC serves more as emotional intimacy but refrain from taking the final steps because they want the MC to live a normal life in this chapter. 

The MC: Her world is crumbling and expanding at the same time, which can make her seem passive since she is a side character in a bigger story. She is also caught in a military campaign which limits how much she is able to accomplish since she is surrounded by skilled fighters. Each Love interests forces her to grow in a different way which makes the intimacy memorable. Each man also is conflicted with duty and honor vs self preservation which they confide in her as she is a third party... your basically the resident counselor. Minor spoilers, some of the cast have survived suicide attempts. 

Knowing the pay off this game is well worth it if you plan to pick up both titles. There is lots of memorable play time.

This game made me wish there was a maybe button as to "do I recommend this game". I ended up going with yes but I do have some disclaimers/thoughts on the game.

#1-This is not a romance game. I went in fully expecting it to be the typical otome game, which in part was my fault. This game is split into two parts (this being the first) meaning that this is the basic background of  your relationship with the characters which basically equates to little to no romance. Don't get me wrong, with some characters you get moments of tension and slight flirting, but overall it's about growing friendships. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, but a total let down if you're expecting romance.
#2- This game is long. As i said, went in expecting romance and about an hour in I was made aware of the two part aspect of the game. Okay. Well i figured I'd just play through this game real quick and then jump into the romantic second installment. Nope. This game dragged. I finished one route in the 12 hour play time I have wracked up and i'm a decently fast reader. And you can't just skip to the next game as you'll lack context. You could probably look up a summary but it just doesn't leave you with the same understanding of even just little details and moments playing this first game provides. This is especially a slap in the face considering how fast the second installment "Edo Blossom" goes by comparatively.

But anyways, you're probably wondering why i recommend it if I have so many complaints. Overall the game was good, just not what I expected. Had I originally not gone into this game expecting the typical romance I don't think I'd have nearly as many complaints. That's why i want to make it very clear what you're getting out of this game. Removing my rose-tinted glasses proved this game to be an endearing and sweet friendship building game which in many (but not all, looking at you Shinpachi) routes planted the seeds of  a soon to grow romance. I think Kyoto Winds is worth the play as long as you fully realize what you're getting into. :)

I bought the original version of Hakuoki for PSP when it was first released in America. I absolutely loved it!  Ever since hearing about Kyoto Winds, I'd hoped for a release on Steam. My wish was granted, thank you Steam! I have played a decent chunk of the beginning so far and below are my impressions of this new version.

Note: Kyoto Winds is NOT the full game of Hakuoki. It has been split in two. I assume this version ends right as the characters leave Kyoto. Part two (Edo Blossoms) is being released spring 2018. With all the added features I personally don't mind the wait. But if you do it's something to keep in mind. Going forward from here:

The translation for this iteration of the game has changed significantly from it's PSP predecessor. Chizuru - the main heroine has a lot more to say and think here. You see the world through her lens now, which can be good or bad. Depending on your preference. Scenarios play out differently as well with added dialouge. It gives a fresh feeling to a farmiliar tale. Slight nitpick ahead. Some of the translation differences I haven't been too keen on but most are spot on. 

Character portraits now blink and their lips move (most of the time) as they speak. It's a nice little detail. It seems hair movement may also come into play down the line, or at least they did in the new opening cinematic. Speaking of characters there are now three new romance options added to the ballot and three additional routes for the characters with smaller roles in the original game. 

The soundtrack change will be known to PSP players immediately. I loved the old score, I really did but the tracks themselves were very short and grew repetative quickly. I found myself turning the music off after a few playthrough routes. Kyoto Winds contains a completely new OST. This new soundtrack has really captured my attention. It's layered and nuanced really setting the tone well. I can't wait to hear more of it in game.

Options: You can adjust the volume level for music voice and sound effects. Furthermore the voice adjusting goes into far more depth than before. Don't like the sound of a particular character's voice? Or is one voice louder than the others?  Now you can adjust character voices individually. I greatly appreciate this!

Overall I'm pleased with the changes that have been made and would recommened this as a worth while purchase to those who have played the original releaase on PSP.

Hakuoki: Kyoto Winds is the first part of a  two part remake of  the orginal Hakuoki: Demons Of The Fleeting Blossoms. You play as Yukimura Chizuru, a girl in search of her father but ended up in the bellies of the Shinsengumi's dark secrets.

I got this game before it went on sale and despite regretting that I could have gotten it for less, I'd say it's totally worth the full price because of how detailed  the game is from the art, background music, and to the voice acting.


The main thing I LOVE about Kyoto Winds (and hakuoki in general) is how slow burn the romance is, allowing me to focus on the actual story without a guy forcing his way onto my character every five seconds. It strays from your casual otome with aggressive men (which I honestly grew out and tired of) and provides a more realistic approach of getting to know each other instead. 

[b] Your character [/b], Yukimura Chizuru, is basically a log... but I found her quite loveable with her willingness to help and wholesome personality. Some may prefer a more active mc, but she's good enough for you to be empathetic towards her and her goals. 

[b] The music and voice acting [/b] is astounding. Not once did I ever think "oh this guy could have done better with another voice". My only problem was at times, Kazama's normal voice volume seems to be hushed compared to others.

[b] Art. [/b]  Despite some weird anatomy and awkward sideview faces sometimes, this otoge still has top notch art compared to other paid ones that wouldnt even bother putting a properly rendered background (you know which game you are). 

[b] The story [/b]  Hakuoki is about the Bakumatsu period and the Shinsengumi. Both Kyoto Winds and Edo Blossoms get pretty history heavy and people just looking for a fun romancey time might not like it. Kyoto Winds has very little romance and instead, focuses on the events that occured during the period. The story somewhat feels a bit rushed at times but the interesting characters make up for it.  For twelve guys, I'm kind of amazed at how different it feels from other otoge with only the stereotypes holding each  love interest. Hakuoki men can each be summed up in one word, but playing the game shows you that it offers more than "Silent type, Playboy type, etc." Every guy has a personality that feels realistic... and all of them lovable. (Though there is one Hakuoki guy that I found quite one dimensional.)

tldr; slow burn romance and no guy tries to sexually force himself on the mc like ten other otoge. 11/10. -1 for the pain and suffering this game has brought me.

While it's definitely not a perfect game, I definitely still recommend it. The description does say it's the first of a two part series - something very apparent by the time you reach the end. It's clear it's not a complete story.

I feel the '80 hours of romance' is a huge overstatement on several fronts. Even though it is necessary to play through multiple times to really get the full story (and it can be fun to uncover all the different moments available based on the choices you make), there's a lot of repeating what you've already read.

The art is hontestly flat out *gorgeous* on all fronts, though. All sprites are well designed, including the side characters. CGs are also beautifully done.

The 'extras' in the cast do have a bit of no-eyes syndrome going on but the protagonist, at least, has a face when she appears in CGs so that's a definitely plus – and it makes the no-eyes extras more forgivable.

There are also a lot of really gorgeous backgrounds. A lot. Because the scenery changes quite a bit, there's a huge variety of different environments and a lot of small details that really add to the experience (such as showing a simple ceiling BG when the protagonist is lying in bed.) It feels like they went to a lot of lengths to ensure the game was visually appealing. The fight sequences are also well done, and are set up in a way that makes them more engaging than just looking at static sprites on static backgrounds. 

The simple animations definitely enhance the experience. And the lip-synch animation is actually done much better than a lot of visual novels. So props there. 

All the love interests I've played so far have distinct personalities. While some characters have similar traits, each one is still unique enough to stand out from the others, which is really nice in a game with so many potential love interests. I think the characters are interesting and, for the most part, likeable. Some characters have clear and interesting development as well, which makes the story fun to read.

The writing, from a technical standpoint, is well done. Things are written clearly, they're easily understandable, though there are a few typographical errors here and there.

But…as I mentioned above. '80 hours'? I just don't see it. 

First of all, there's not much 'romance' to speak of - much less 80 hours of it. Most of this part of the story focuses on the political goings on around the protagonist so she actually spends comparatively little time with whatever specific love interest you're pursuing. What scenes she does have tend to be more on the platonic side - there are exceptions and some routes have more obvious hints at romance than others. These moments are often short and don't really go far beyond hints until the latter chapters of a few routes.

But  I just struggle to see how there's 80 hours of content at all, due to the sheer amount of re-reading previously read content. It seems extremely exaggerated at best (unless the 80 hours refers to parts one and two together. In which case, it seems misleading to list the complete amount what is only part of the story).

Personally, I find the story to be the weakest part of this visual novel. While the characters are interesting, fun, cute, and often intriguing…

They frequently get a bit lost in a story that's trying to juggle too many events, too many sub-plots and a too-huge time scale. Characterization and relationship development often suffer while the story tries to cram a huge amount of historical upheaval into a fairly condensed game experience.

To be safe, I'll put the rest below spoiler tags:

[spoiler]The amount of time this game covers is at least four years. That means a lot of time skips –often months at a time, over really a really short amount of play time. This rapid jumping through time causes a sort of strange situation where the story both feels like it's moving way too fast and dragging on way too slowly. 

For instance, many characters (including the protagonist, frankly) show relatively little character development despite the amount of time that passes. Even though they're aging four years - sometimes going from child to adult - there is not much emotional maturing that happens. The MC is as naive and innocent four years later, as she is when she first joins the Shinsengumi. And that is after living alongside seasoned samurai, helping out on missions and being surrounded by death.

There are other issues with the time scale not seeming to match up with story development. It's hard to believe that hints of romance developing in her first months with the Shinsengumi remain mere hints four years later. How does a relationship not develop at all during that amount of time?

There's also a lot of ambiguity as to what exactly she's doing during that four years. She clearly isn't learning to use her sword (she's as useless in battle during the final chapters as she is at the start.) Some routes indicate she is acting as a medic but this isn't addressed at all if you focus on other characters. And either way, she's never really shown acting as a medic. It mostly happens off-screen or in conversation.  Like other things, it feels glossed over and cast to the side in favor of focusing on the upheaval and struggles of the Shinsengumi as a whole.

The story just didn't seem to be able to balance the events going on with actual character development. 

The demon/fury sub-plot kind of comes out of left field. As if historical fiction wasn't interesting enough on its own so they had to make the main character special by being not human - and throw some Vampires in for dramatic effect. Some aspects of it aren't handled extremely well, particularly in some routes. It typically only surfaces when it seems convenient for stirring up some drama. I also felt that some elements of this plot struggled to find any sort of internal logic to follow and were a bit all over the place.

This is another plot that is handled better when you focus on some love interests than on others. But the fact that some routes feel so much better balanced while others are lacking gets a bit frustrating at times.[/spoiler]

All these elements together cause the story to sometimes buckle under its own weight. I found myself really dissatisfied, at times, with how sluggish things were moving and at others I was frustrated because it felt like I was just skimming the surface of what could be a really detailed story.

All of that may seem like a serious gripe but this visual novel definitely has parts that are enjoyable. There are some fantastically lovable characters, and it's definitely a joy to just look at. Seriously. The art's [i] really[/i] beautiful.

For those thinking of buying the game, I recommend waiting until it's on sale. Lovely as it is, I don't think the story content warrants the full price. Despite its length, it very much feels like a prologue or set up to a longer story. Which explains the skips through time and glossing over of certain story elements and the lack of development in some areas. It feels very much like it's just prepping you for what's to come. 

All of that's fine, honestly. But I wouldn't personally pay full price for something that doesn't really read like a full game/story.

This review will be a little strange, since well... i am a straight man. The main reason i played this to take a look at Shinsengumi story and overall Shogunate vs Imperialists war. Being pretty fluent in Japanese History i wanted to see a writers approach on Fall of Shogunate. That being said i will point to an elephant in the room right away...
The Main Character is awful. She has no personality, no "face", no nothing. She is like Pointman from the F.E.A.R game - just a plot tool and players "eyes". Aside from that she is stupid and practically a log. Not going to spoil anything, but she is basically a plot driver. MC doing something stupid -> story event happens. Yukimura is as flat as one can imagine. You can insert ANYONE on her place and nothing will change, since she is not a character.
The Writing. 
It is not good nor bad. I looks like they had two writers. One is very skilled in Japanese History and the other who is a freelancer and a graphomaniac. "Big Game" part of the story which involves politics and historical events, samurai way of life etc. is very engaging and interesting, but as soon as we dive into mystery, demons and romantics writing falls short, so low that is makes me cringe. Awfully common and hackneyed cliched plot twists, i can bet a grand i saw it like 9999 times already. Cliche on top of cliche and especially "dialogues about food", bland and useless for "Grand Plot" characters. At some point it falls so flat that i thought this plot is beyond saving, but than THE GOOD writer takes the driver seat again and last chapter was so good that i had no way but to give this game a like. Not going to spoil it, but the main villain will make you hate him so much, that you would want to rip his head apart, and last battle is simply excellent. I know all this mystery BS is designed to give the MC the reason to stay among Shinsengumi and make romances but it really feels... off and boring to death. Not to mention cliched and plain stupid. However "The Big Game" part of the story is very good, and can be interesting for anyone who want to take a look at the last years of Shogunate or simply has interest in Japanese history.
The Art
Pretty OK. Seen better (FAR better). But it is good, all characters drawn attractive and careful. However it is obvious that original art is meant to be displayed at 720p (PS3) and was upscaled. Characters designs and backgrounds are amazing, though. 
The Characters. 
From historical standpoint... well you know the answer already. From fictional and dramatic side however, they are GENERALLY good. Some of them more interesting than others, but overall they are good written and i sure all routes are interesting enough (except main villain, who the hell want to romance him anyway ?). Most of them can be related in some ways and you are going to miss them (if you know what i mean) [spoiler] when they will die [/spoiler]. Their impact on the story (and "parts" of the story) varies, some are engaged in "Big Game" and some are more into mystical and fictional side.
Since i had little to no interest in romances (however i somehow started Hijikata's route) and my answers was based on what i would do in situations, i cant judge this game as Otome fairly. But if you want a Date Sim and a game about "pick up a boy" this is a wrong door. 90% of the game is NOT about the romances. Romance part is contained in Edo Blossoms, and since i have no interest in it, because historical part of the story is ended here, i cant judge it either. I don't have much to say besides that Hakuouki is a classic that must be played by all otome game lovers. I don't really understand why they split the game into two parts at all, so keep in mind I'm talking about the whole game (both halves) when I say this. 

The new characters are really charming, got my gripes with some bullshit storyline aspects in some of them both new and old actually, but they're amazing. Switching from other otome games to this I really felt this as more involving at least character-wise. Like for example Code:Realize's story is way better constructed than Hakuouki's but the characters aren't as layered as Hakuouki in the long run (and here I'm also speaking of the sequels/alternate stories), so the romances turn a bit too cringy and cheesy for my liking, because of how "perfect" (in different degrees, I really like Saint Germain and Impey, but Finis took the crown =w=), most of them seem to be, while characters in Hakuouki aren't dislikable by any means, but they got flaws, like Kazama's cynicism, Okita's sassiness and emotional dishonesty, Souma's tendency to always self-guilt, Sanan's ability to not talk and get misunderstood often (though some of his grey morals really ain't helping either) etc. 

This is also one of those old-fashioned otome games that tend to not be made as often anymore, where you have to really struggle to get the guy you want by using the trial and error of multiple choices adventures, you don't have a main menu where you can choose a route, and I really REALLY miss that gameplay aspect of it. (Edo Blossoms does but it's assumed you played Kyoto Winds which is where the work is mainly focused on)

Another thing I really like is how they made it easier to obtain all CGs and endings, not by save/load files that you had to make yourself at convenient places, but by allowing you to directly load the chapter you need with the stats you need. There's some charm in figuring it all out yourself, games like Heart no kuni no Alice heavily rely on save files, but that can become often tedious and most Hakuouki's endings aren't that worth it to go to that extent in my opinion (besides the Good ends obviously, with some exceptions, mainly Okita Souji. *insert a biased cough here*).

Some downsides would be the already mentioned bulshit storyline threads, like sometimes I just feel like the writers had no idea what to do with certain characters so they went on crack one day and were like "ah yeah, this totally makes sense!" (Hachiro and his whole arm situation comes to mind right now, like what. why. how??, Shinpachi to me was another problem, but in the opposite way, while Hachiro's route tended to be complicated and eyebrow raising af, Shinpachi had almost nothing going for him besides a "big bro/little sis" dynamic between him and Chizuru and while that doesn't necessarily have to be bad I also wondered why the story needed to be told in the first place besides just ticking him off the checklist of available samurai bachelors). 
That said, the second downside is Chizuru herself. While not entirely aggravating at all times, she unfortunately joins the dull, useless rank of otome heroines that expresses the wish to improve but she never does. Probably one of her best versions was in Yamazaki's route, where she expressed how while she found she was bad at fighting, she tried her best to fight in different ways, like using her medical skills and I could really see how hard she tried, besides just being the guy's emotional support as she's usually reduced to. I liked her attitude when in pair with Kazama or Okita too, maybe those sort of personalities just make her twitch enough to show that she's got character, which is always a plus for me lol.  However I think most of the guys and the story make up for it enough, especially if you're a history nerd or have interest in Japan's last samurai time period. 
 
Anyway, the game (+Edo blossoms) ain't that expensive at the time of this review, so I really recommend trying to go for it if you like otome games but never had the chance to try out Hakuouki. Also excuse my chaotic review, I'm really just writing this out of nostalgia and wanted to express myself somewhat. I might edit this later on. 

PS: I hope Idea Factory will stop milking this series. Unless they localize stuff like Hakuouki Reimeiroku and all the other Hakuouki mini games lol (Idea Factory, if you're reading this *wink wink*). But if they don't stop i'm sure we're gonna fall back into it like the trash we are. lol

[b]Hakuouki: Kyoto Winds[/b] is a remaster of the game "Hakuouki", originally released on PS2 in 2008. I was pleasantly surprised that there are no kisses, words of love or erotic content, only hints. This is a naive, in some places stupid story about friendship, self-sacrifice in the name of duty and love. I as a person with a heart of stone, can say for sure - nothing caused my tears no matter how awful the ending was. I guess, the game is mainly oriented towards romantic and dreamy female players, and it would be foolish to demand something brutal, terrible and cruel to a nervous tic. 
[i]There are 12 routes (three endings for each character). In total: [b]36 endings.[/b]

Recommendable  routes(IMHO): Hijikata, Harada, Toudou, Nagakura, Iba, Yamazaki, Sakamoto and Kazama's.

[u] Pros: [/u]
+ 12 romanceable guys,  so you'll definitely have your favorite at the end of the story.

+ Fascinating  CG's. I bet artist sold his soul to the Devil for such talent. I wish I could draw like that one day.

+ Lenght. My first walkthrough of Hijikata's route took about  10 hours. 
+ Mini- encyclopedia. If something causes questions, the game will explain.

[u]Cons: [/u]
- To play other route you must skip tons of text you read before. 
- Cannot skip credits after route was finished. I don't mind to read  it at first, but I decided  to beat up all achievements, so pretty annoying . It was fixed at "Edo Blossoms".

- Some glitches(black streaks) in Sakamoto's route after using "force skip".
- Chizuru. She's a typical Mary Sue with ultimate abilities, such as fast healing of wounds and making tea.More than 50% of the game she complains that she is not a human and completely useless  to the Shinsengumi. The MC, Chizuru Yukimura, heads to Kyoto to search for her father, finding herself attacked by mad men before they are cut down by members of the Shinsengumi who take her into custody for interrogation. Upon learning that she is a girl and the daughter of a doctor who developed the Water of Life elixir that turns those that drink it into invincible blood lusting berserkers called 'Rasetsu', the Shinsengumi decide to keep her as an aide in their search. During her stay with the Shinsengumi, she discovers that there is a lot more going on with the shogunate, but she also discovers secrets about her identity and those around her.

Kyoto Winds marks the beginning of Chizuru's journey. There exist spin-offs of the franchise, but unfortunately Steam offers Kyoto Winds and its sequel, Edo Blossoms, only.

This game blew my mind. 
I bought it on sale, not really expecting much but damn. I should probably mention that I have no former experience or knowledge of the Hakuoki series (I've somehow missed it through all these years), yet I was equally, or perhaps even more impressed with this series than those who have played it before. 

Firstly, the artwork is in a league of its own. I've played a few visual novels but very few, especially PC ones, match up to the artwork in this. It's simply beautiful. The colouring in the CGs and proportions of the characters are amazing, unlike the many anime-inspired art pieces with their overly-lanky proportions and flat colouring.

The voice acting in this is also breath taking. If you're not a fan of it, there's always the option to switch it off but holy cow, I love it. I'm a fairly fast reader, so I almost always finish reading before the part gets read out but the thing is, I found myself waiting for the voice acting to finish because I just love their voices - Kazama's in particular. 

One thing I will say is that this game is pretty history and plot heavy, not much romance if any in it (though different routes differ slightly on this), so if you're getting this in the hopes of the typical cheesy, k-drama romance, you're out of luck. I personally love history but have never really been interested in East Asian history, especially Japanese history. This game changed that. 
There's also a lot of Japanese terms and keywords which are kept logged in the encylopedia - I found the sheer number of them to be confusing, but as I replayed the game to experience the different routes, I gradually got used to it and made more sense the more I played. The same could be said for the number of characters. There's 12 guys to choose from, plus a fair few side characters, which made it hard at the start to remember who was who (bearing in mind I have no prior knowledge of this game and have very little experience with the Japanese language). Of course, this wasn't so much as an issue when I replayed it more. 

If I had to be nit-picky, I would also put the MC's personality down as more of a con than a pro. It can be a little infuritating how unable she is to stand up for and protect herself, always relying on the members of the Shinsengumi. It's as if she's playing damsel in distress and is simply doting on guys to save her, instead of actually attempting to defend herself. [spoiler]She does actually learn some swordsmanship techniques through Kondou in a number of routes, albeit not much, but enough for self defence. Even so, we do not see her put these new skills in use at all further in the storyline.[/spoiler] Her character plays by many tropes in otome games - special snowflake, damsel in distress, a little dense at the best of times - and if those tropes are really something you can't stand, this may not be the best series for you. However, being completely honest from my standpoint, I've played many otome games with far worse MCs, whose traits are far more exaggerated. Although the MC in this game is a little infuriating and annoying at times, it's not really a factor that affected my enjoyment of this game and because of this, I still hold this game very highly. 

On the whole, I think this game has good replay value and I would highly recommend this. There are some repetitive bits that get a little tedious, but nothing the cheeky skip button can't fix. Overall, it's incredibly well thought through and is definitely up there in the realm of visual novels and otome. Even if you're not into the otome stuff, I would still suggest giving this a go. It's worth every penny, even if not on sale.

This review contains mild spoilers so be aware before reading furthur.

Regarding route selection, I highly recommend progressing by the order of the record, as in Hijikata>Souji>Saito etc, with Kazama definitely should be the last, as more of the story is unfolded as you progress through the characters. At the end of the day, it's your choice, but I do think if you, says, choose Sanan first before playing all other characters, it would affect your enjoyment of other routes due to certain details about key characters being revealed in his route. Btw, some characters are done dirty, not only they suffer bad fate in other routes, but have less CGs as well. No fair.

The protagonist, by default, has a somewhat flat personality, depends on the route/choices, she is either being very active and joins various activities, or being relatively quiet and stays inside most of the time. I have been told this is to make it easier for players assimilate themselves with the MC, so that's that. Generally she's a positive person though. One thing I definitely dislike about her, and female oni/demon in general [spoiler]is that aside from accelerate healing, they are virtually no different than normal people, while the male ones are so freaking strong.[/spoiler]

As for the story, due to this game being a buildup, there are a lot of overlapping contents between routes, and as much as I like the voice-acting, by the 3rd route I was kinda bored of it and just waiting for the text to finished being skipped. It follows the actual Shinsengumi history quite closely too, so if you like their history, it's a bonus. Each romance target has different problem and requires different thing from the MC, so the unique parts of each route is quite enjoyable.

My biggest problem with the game is the volume, yes, I know it's weird, but hear me out. On both speaker and headset, if I set the volume so that normal dialogue can be heard properly, the yelling is way too loud while the mumbling is almost impossible to hear. Even more so with Sanan, his normal speech is hard to hear enough due to how soft-spoken he is, when he's mumbling I can barely hear anything, and that's with both the in-game's and computer's volume being set to highest (which again, almost destroyed my eardrum, figuratively). This problem carries over to Edo Blossoms too.

Second problem, and this is probably me being nitpicky is the translation. Most of it is very good, but naturally a lot, and I mean a lot of nuances, especially about the characters' relationship, are lost. Example: I don't understand why sometimes they switch first and last name of the characters when translating the dialogue. Or when Kondou calls Okita "Sougo", it uses "Souji" instead. If anything, it should remains "Sougo" and being explained. Also sometimes they extend one sentence by a lot while reducing a long dialogue to just 1 short sentence.

Which brings me to the last problem which is related to the translation, the encyclopedia. I understand that the game probably keeps all the same vocab explanation to its original Japanese version, which some words do require explanation (eg SatChou is Satsuma-Choushuu alliance, but in Japan it would just be called SatChou) and maybe its main function isn't to explain the meaning but to help you keep track of the terms. However, a lot of the words, when being translated to English, is already self-explanatory, so you basically have a lot of it being explain like "Satsuma Choushuu alliance is the alliance between Satsuma and Choushuu" or something along that line.

tl:dr Overall good game with play with Edo Blossoms, as a standalone it sucks. Give it a try if you like Shinsengumi and ikemen.

The first thing to note to anyone wishing to enjoy this game is to understand this is part one of two games. By purchasing this game, you are purchasing only half a product, in my personal opinion. This game should be treated wholeheartedly as an introduction to these characters and the build-up to the central narrative. I enjoyed this game, but I can only recommend it when it is on sale, arguably a deep sale.

 There is a good story, solid characters, and seriously great music here but it holds itself back in my opinion. The thing that holds this back to a 5/10 (while worth playing, don't get me wrong, it is a decent read) is first, as mentioned previously, this is half of a product-- and secondly....what the hell happened with the translation? It feels so utterly bare-bones. When characters aren't awkwardly cursing and emotionally confusing the tones of normal conversation, then the rest of the piece feels so stripped of the atmosphere, tone, and much-needed fill-in details that usually elevate the reading of visual novels. I wouldn't say it ruins the experience but it drops its score by several points for me compared to better visual novels of its kind. It's a shame and rather bizarre to see because there is a complex story being told here in the native language, but man, the English translation couldn't keep it together. 

5/10, I guess, deep sale, and I really hope more effort was put into the second half, "Edo Blossoms".

My favourite Otome game, bar none.  This game has beautiful art, an excellent soundtrack, and complex stories that are rich with true-to-history detail.  This is a game best enjoyed by those who enjoy a more true-to-life historical romance; be prepared for a "slow burn" type of approach with most of the romanceable guys.

**Very Important**:  This is only the FIRST HALF of the full story for each guy.  This means more reading and fewer modern "romance" elements, at least in Kyoto Winds, the localized version of Hakuoki Shinkai: Kaze no Shou (the game was released in 2 parts in Japan as well).  Barring the supernatural elements, this game stays relatively faithful to the feel and standards of the historical setting, which is 1864 Japan (i.e., Victorian times, from an English-world perspective).  The second half of the game, with the final route endings, is Hakuoki Edo Blossoms (out Spring 2018).

If you read the reviews, you will see that what most people dislike is that the game ends halfway through the main story lines.  This was unavaoidable because this game has twice as many routes (romance interests) as the original and adds content even for the original characters.  If it is important to you to have complete routes from the get-go, I recommend playing the mobile version of the game (Android and iOS) or the PS3 version (still my favourite version, as it has so much fun extra content).  You will only get 6 routes instead of 12 though!

PROS:  One of the best otome games out there *if* you like historical drama and don't mind a slow burn romance style.  Good music, lovely art, characters you think about even after you're done playing.  Lots of choice!

CONS:  As in Japan, this game is only the first half of each story.  The common route makes up a big percentage of this game; while there are lots of choices and characters, you will find yourself with lots of rereading / skipping to do.  Also, I did not find the game as well-translated as it could have been.  I miss the translation values of the original game.

I played the 3DS version of Hakuoki years ago, and had my eye on this one and it's sequel, Edo Blossoms, for some time due to there being extra routes for new characters. I was not disappointed.
The new characters are as  well written as the originals, and both their design and backstories fit perfectly with the preexisting characters. The sprites for the originals have been altered slightly, and new content has been added to their routes, so although playing through their individual storylines felt a little nostalgic, it didn't feel as much of a repetition of the 3DS version as I had expected it to. I was excited that they had added Nagakura as a love interest in this game (he wasn't in the 3DS version), and finally being able to play through his route was awesome.
The artwork, from sprites, to CGs, to backgrounds are still stunning, and the soundtrack is as good as I remember, and often fits the events occurring perfectly. The characters are all voiced (excluding the protagonist), and the voice acting is great quality. 
The plot is interesting, and their are plenty of choices to explore some diverse content. Also, there is some amount of historical accuracy for the time period, and an in-game encyclopedia explains terms that may be unfamiliar. The romances don't feel forced, and feel unique to each character.
There are some points where the translations can be a little lacking, whether this is because of a missing word, something repeated, or a phrase that doesn't make sense, but they are easy to ignore. 
The controls seemed a little odd at first, but users can set them to what they like.
I'd recommend this game to anyone who has previously enjoyed otome games, as Hakuoki is one of the best available. This version has only improved upon what was already a great game, so I would also recommend to anyone who had played a previous Hakuoki title.

I would like to begin this review with this: you have to buy both Kyoto Winds and Edo Blossoms in order to get the full story. Kyoto Winds covers the first half of the original game +new routes of other characters +3 new characters that give you interesting perspectives. Edo Blossoms cover the individual routes and its full romances. What KW cover is 85% common route and the 15% being the start of the 'official' character route, hence, you need to get EB to finish the story completely.

This is my first 'commercial' otome game and I believe that Hakuoki as a whole lives up to its legacy. For what its worth, it's a good historical fantasy as it highlights the significant events of pre-meiji period and the fall of the Tokugawa Shogun. What I like most about this is how we are given the opportunity of different perspectives of these events through Chizuru's lens and each character. Particularly the introduction of the 3 new characters. Funnily enough, I seemed to have learned a few things about this part of Japan's history through this game.

I will say though, as some reviews have mentioned, romance is not the focus simply because KW covers the common route of the original game. Not to say that it is not romantic; the romance exists in a slow burn between shared moments with the characters and Chizuru. If I were to scale the level from romantic to platonic routes (in KW) then:
1. Iba
2. Yamazaki
3. Harada
4. Todou
5. Saito
6. Souji
7. Sakamoto
8. Sanan
9. Kazama
10. Hijikata
11. Souma
12. Nagakura
I mean, the scale is subjective depending on your taste, but the sequel game definitely covers the romantic parts of each route.

The issues I have with this game is perhaps the lack of exploiting Iba's and Sakamoto's perspective of the events of pre-Boshin war. Particularly the failing Shogunate and the dive in details of the oni clans. Because we are limited to Chizuru's perspective, we only catch glimpses of their point of view towards the two things.
Another issue was Nagakura's route, as the plot cannot decide whether it wanted him to be a platonic bro-sis dynamic or romantic. I would have been satisfied if it did go platonic, but by the end of KW it couldn't decide where it wanted to go.

The order of routes to play through? Honestly, go blind and see where the choices take you. I was surprised I landed on Iba first and did not regret it. Hijikata's route may not come off as romantic, but most of his route acts as a the main foundation of the game's storyline.
I do recommend it best to get the game in the full set on a steam sale. It's worth in both full and half-price, but it'd be better to buy it in a bundle.

A lot of otome games don't take the time to really develop the characters of the love interests, however, that is not the case in Hakuoki. It really takes the time to explore and develop the characters of the boys and all of them are quite pleasant and charming in their own way. 

The story is also very interesting and doesn't allow you to get bored easily. I'm not sure how historically accurate it actually is (as it is supposedly based on true events), but I do know that I enjoyed the story a lot. 

Contrary to popular belief, I actually found the protagonist decent. (for otome games standards) Yes, she was physically weak and perhaps not very intelligent, but she also showed a lot of bravery sometimes and there were moments where she showed a lot of emotional strength and made some insightful observations. She was definitely better than the protagonists in some other similar games I have played or at least that's how it seemed to me. 

The art is beautiful and the music is superb. In general, it is a very well made game, that's why it's also so expensive. 

If you buy this game, keep in mind that you should also buy Hakuoki: Edo Blossoms which is the sequel and very important for the story.

[h1]Please note that this game is the first part of a two-part story. It's also a remake.[/h1]

In Hakuoki, you get to play as Chizuru, a girl who is looking for her father in Kyoto. She ends up staying with the members of the Shinsengumi, a feared police force that existed during the Bakumatsu period in Japan.

The choices you make in the game will lead you towards a path where you end up with one of the 12 available bachelors.

One important thing to keep in mind is that the game ends halfway through the story. Up to that point, there's also not much romance, but more of a buildup of the relationships and events that happen during the story. Hakuoki: Edo Blossoms is the second part of the story and includes much more romance. I'd recommend playing a route in Kyoto Winds and then switching over to Edo Blossoms to continue the story since you can pick the route you want from the start in the second part.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

The gameplay is like any visual-based novel, you read through the story and you get to make some choices every now and then. All the lines except the narrative and main character are voiced by good actors/actresses and the background music is also beautiful. There are some characters that may sound a bit louder than the others though (like Shinpachi) so keep that in mind.

It's really easy to immerse yourself, partly because of the stunning visuals but also because the story is quite long and complex. Most of the events and characters in the game are historically correct and you can learn a lot of Japanese history this way. However, some parts are fairly linear and play out the same in a lot of the routes and it takes some time to really branch out into the unique parts for a specific character.

All characters have their own story and they are not copy-pastes of each other. You may dislike a route or two but I personally find most of them enjoyable. I will not dwell too much about the characters though because this topic can be very subjective.

The only bugs and errors I found were some minor spelling errors and the lips of the characters being out of synch when speaking. I also had to use my gamepad to change the resolution and to play it in fullscreen.

[h1]My final conclusion[/h1]

Hakuoki is personally one of my favorite visual novels, mostly because of the historical setting (Bakumatsu period) and because I love stories with samurai warriors. It's among one of the first few otome games that were localized in the west, and it's a quite good introduction to the genre for those who are new to otome. I played the 3DS version which was shorter and had less content, so the extra material in this game made me quite happy. Hakuoki can feel like a drag sometimes though because the common route is quite long and there are so many bachelors to choose from. The amount of bachelors can also be considered a positive, since you're bound to find at least a handful that you really like. As for the MC, Chizuru is not the most enjoyable MC because she feels too meek but considering the historical setting and her young age, she is at least realistic as a character. Nevertheless, I feel that the story, visuals and voice acting make up for the small downsides. I enjoyed this game a lot and I feel that it should be played by anyone already interested in otome as well as people who just discovered the genre.

Hakuoki is an absolute otome classic, being one of the first and most popular localized otome releases in the west. You could say that this game walked so that many of the amazing English otomes we have nowadays could run. I was intrigued by the game and its story so I did some research and found that most of the characters and the events that take place (aside from the obvious fantasy elements) are real, and the historical accuracy is astounding. As many other reviews have stated as well, Hakuoki: Kyoto Winds is only half of the entire Hakuoki experience. I decided to write this review before playing Edo Blossoms so that my opinions would be based solely off of this first part.

Due to the fact that Kyoto Winds is only the first part the romance is, unfortunately, pretty lacking. I imagine the second part will give a lot more to work with in that department but if you're in it for a steamy love story then there are some pretty slim pickings here. Of course there are still some superb CG artworks depicting cute scenes between the protag and her chosen LI, but these tender moments are few and far between[spoiler] the closest thing you get to a kiss is a peck on the forehead from one of the characters...[/spoiler]. The plot itself is fun for the first playthrough, if at times a bit too heavy with the political talk that can seem to drag on endlessly. The fantasy elements served to keep things interesting, while the interactions between titular characters helped offset the boring politics and bring some life back into the story.

Apparently, the original release had only six love interests, while this one boasts a whopping twelve. That's a heck of a lot of men to romance, so you're bound to find at least one that you like... But, on the flip side, you'll probably also find one or two that you'd rather skip. As a completionist myself, this was not an option, and I strove to get every single CG and every ending for all of the characters. My top three were definitely Hijikata, Chikage, and Sakamoto. Hijikata's felt like the game's intended "main route" and so there was a lot of love put into it, while Chikage actually had the shortest route but his character was one of the most interesting. I liked Sakamoto for the amount of romance in his route that well-exceeded the others just due to the kind of character he is. This otome actually has more of a "linear" gameplay style where all of the routes follow the same exact story, just with individual scenes occurring with your chosen LI, so there is a lot of skipping involved. I found Yamazaki's and Shinpachi's routes to be the biggest slogs to get through as I didn't really like either character but your mileage may vary.

As for the heroine herself... She was okay. I didn't have strong opinions either way, but I do feel like there was squandered potential with her character. Rant: [spoiler]Despite being a pure-blooded demon like Chikage and Amagiri and the others, Chizuru has no supernatural abilities to speak of aside from fast healing. While the others flaunted their superhuman strength, speed, stamina, and agility, Chizuru (and even the other female demon Sen) were lacking these things entirely. The heroine even carries around a blade with her at all times and it is said that she can use it in self defense, yet I can count maybe one time in the entire game where she actually successfully lands a hit on somebody, and even then it's hardly a fatal one. I suspect this has something to do with the way that women are seen in Japanese society, attributing to the fact that none of the female characters seem to be at all useful in a fight here, but I digress. Whatever the reasoning may be, she got talked up a bit too much for how useless she ultimately ended up being.[/spoiler] Aside from these complaints she was very much just the typical otome protagonist: is nice, gullible, wants everybody to be happy, has no talent other than traditionally feminine things like cooking/sewing, etc, and gets protected a lot. A tired trope, to be sure, but luckily not a dealbreaker for me.

The artwork, music, and voice acting were exceptional, as expected. However, there were a few times where some characters or sound effects were WAY too loud and grating to the point where it would cause the mic to get all fuzzy when a man would shout something. Shinpachi was the worst offender for this, and there was this one sound effect of villagers talking in the background that looped way too quickly and was super distracting, but thankfully I think it only showed up a couple of times. Just be prepared to have to pull your headphones away from your ears once in a while, while having to subsequently turn the volume back up once Chikage appears on screen (seriously why was this mans so quiet???). So yeah, aside from the sound design not being absolutely stellar, there were also a few typos and repeated phrases throughout the game that would pop up in the text boxes. Not enough to call the translation bad - far from it - but enough that they would assuredly appear a noticeable amount of times in every route. Thankfully there were no major grammatical errors to speak of; overall, entirely forgivable imo.

It feels very traditional and beautifully crafted.. It flows as if it were unfolding to the hands of fate. The story is a masterpiece of vocal acting, rich characterisation and emotional impact. The romance is there and combined with the deep and unmoving historical setting…  It is subtle yet powerfully striking in its intent; its effect. Those who have said that Kyoto Winds does not focus on romance… have probably not  paid too much attention. Romance is the focus of the story… it is truly an otome romance game even in this first part… The ability to remain realistic..  heightened the romantic atmosphere in simplistic and sophisticated ways.

The men of the shinsengumi have been enlivened and immortalised in a haunting way and this becomes more clear as the story progresses. The honour of the samurai... is uncovered from the faded history of the last days of the Shogunate rule.... Over 260 years and even more  centuries before the Tokugawa era, going back and spanning back to the sengoku era and before, there were good men from Japan. from ordinary backgrounds  who became proud samurai warriors and possessed swords that were held in the name of honour… not madness or evil.  ... Their strength had a place in their realm for hundreds of years  and their hearts were filled with bravery and the inability to back down in the face of death. They wanted to do something courageous and becoming part of the shinsengumi was the pathway they chose… Set in the final years of the shogunate era… Hakuoki is a tale that has captured the essence of the chivalry of the samurai and has in effect delivered through the fictional  median of an otome game… the personal private moments that perhaps… even may speak in a shadow of a whisper of how these samurai men may have felt  and what they may have believed…. Their dreams and their defeats, during the crushing days of the end of the shogunate era. They had no voice…so  one can only guess how they must have felt when their very means of existence came crashing down around them… Hakuoki in a way sheds tears for them.

The power of Japanese storytelling is certainly something that is portrayed from this visual interactive novel. The interactive elements… allow for the player to be part of the last moments of this poetic time of history long forgotten.. A candle about to flicker away… 

For the majority… The initial  interest to play will be based on Hakuoki being an otome/romance game…. But the rich history is sure to capture your attention too and immerse you into the past that Hakuoki seeks to paint … allowing for a rather thorough adventure. 

The voice acting is really brilliant. One of the twelve bachelors, iba hachiro, for example, is voiced by Mamoru Miyano who is famous for having voiced Light Yagami in Death note… 

Overall certainly this otome game is to be highly recommended … Hakuoki is one of the finest otome games made.

Now, onto the review. Hakuoki is a very popular series of otome games that has gotten various rewrites and ports throughout the years. It's extremely popular in Japan, and it's known for being what truly brought otome and visual novels to the west as a niche market medium that's only gotten more and more popular since. 

This version of Hakuoki has 12 routes, and they're as follows (written in family name, given name): Hijikata Toshizo, Okita Souji, Saito Hajime, Toudou Heisuke, Harada Sanosuke, Chikage Kazama... (those are the original routes!) then we have three routes of characters already introduced in the original storyline, they are: Sanan Keisuke, Nagakura Shinpachi, Yamazaki Susumu. Then, to top it all off, there's three new routes: Iba Hachiro, Souma Kazue, and Sakamoto Ryouma. The final route possible is Yukimura (you!) alone, which would make it 13... but it really isn't a route honestly, you're just more or less along for the ride. 

Each route offers different perspectives and events (more so in Edo Blossoms than here) but it's still well worth it to play each route that interests you. The only downside to doing so is having to replay the common route present in this game, Kyoto Winds has a very long common route with a branching narrative to whichever bachelor you decide to pursue... or end up pursuing by chance.

There's enough eligible men in this where anyone can find someone who interests them, but if I'm being completely honest... there's not much romance in Kyoto Winds, it's mainly a focus on the historical aspects of the Shinsengumi and their journey up until the point they leave for Edo. 

There's some fantasy implemented to change things up, of course... I don't want to spoil anything, but it's definitely an interesting take on something you'd expect to be overdone. 

The way this has been translated is really good, especially relative to other visual novel releases on Steam. Don't get me wrong, there's the occasional oddly worded sentence or spelling mistake, but it isn't common to see throughout any of the routes, very rarely do they stick out. 

All in all, if you enjoy historical visual novels or otome games, this is well worth the price. There's plenty of men to choose from, this incorporates some bonus content from previous releases, and the art is absolutely gorgeous from the sprites to the CGs to the opening and ending movies.

You can see this review as the first part of a summarized review of [b][i]Hakuoki: Kyoto Winds[/i][/b] and [b][i]Hakuoki: Edo Blossoms[/i][/b], because basically everything I wrote here can be easily applied on both games. Everything worked perfectly fine for me, I've never experienced any crashes, bugs or similar issues while playing. The exe.file was missing at the launch of [b][i]Hakuoki: Kyoto Winds[/i][/b], but they fixed it within four hours. I was really looking forward to a remastered version of this outstandingly great Visual Novel, and especially to the Steam release, because I never really enjoyed, or got used to playing Otome, or any other games on handheld consoles. 

First, I would like to mention the significant differences in comparison to the English localization of [b][i]Hakuōki: Shinsengumi Kitan[/i][/b] that was firstly released for [i]PSP[/i] back in 2009, known as [b][i]Hakuoki: Demon of the Fleeting Blossom[/i][/b]. The English version of the main game was also released for [i]Nintendo DS[/i], and later for [i]PS3[/i] with a few differences, additional content, and several improvements here and there. I'll refer mostly to the [i]PSP[/i] version since I've spent more time on that one, and I assume that most people which played Hakuoki before, played the [i]PSP[/i] version as well. 

The graphic quality greatly improved, compared to [b][i]Hakuoki: Demon of the Fleeting Blossom[/i][/b], so has the sound quality and the quality of the CG’s as well. Hakuoki takes place in the Tokugawa/Edo Period and makes use of the names of the most famous Shinsengumi members, that once actually existed. The whole story is very close to the previously real-life events and it will lead you through a lot of knowledge of japan history. I don't think that [b][i]Hakuoki: Kyoto Winds[/i][/b], is nearly 80 hours long since there is a lot of skipping if you're using [i]Skip Read[/i] after playing through 2-3 routes. More or less than 30 hours is a realistic time, to reach 100%.

Hakuoki Kyoto Winds is a good historical visual novel filled with a variety of interesting characters. Despite the lack of romance that one might expect from an otome game, the relationships are still compelling and you end up really caring about the characters. The gradual process of getting close with other characters feels natural. The plot is pretty good, following the Shinsengumi’s history over the course of 4-5 years and Chizuru’s (the MC's) experience living with them. 

There are some exciting action scenes, fun villains, and a bit of mystery regarding the MC’s background. Choices do matter in this game, as they determine whose route you end up on and whether you get a good, normal, or bad ending. A little butterfly icon pops up to let you know you’ve made a choice leading to a happy ending, which is handy. The different character routes don’t really diverge too much from the core story. The first 2-3 chapters are pretty similar regardless of route, though there are different side scenes that happen. A lot of Chapter 4 and 100% of Chapter 5 and the Epilogue will be unique to the route. The repetition can be a bit much, especially with 12 routes, though there is a skip button. You do tend to learn different information in each route, so aside from hanging out with a different character you also get a deeper understanding of the story.

Though Hijikata is the recommended first route, I would highly recommend not doing his route first if you would like to not hate the MC. The core story was good, but it was painful playing as the MC (the girl needs to get some self-respect and stop apologizing for her very existence, good grief). It took me a playing a few more routes before I actually started to like her. Her character can vary a bit by route, but I appreciate how when she decides to trust someone she is very steadfast and doesn’t waver. She will stand up for others (and sometimes herself *sigh*), and she cares deeply about the (future) love interest. She doesn’t have a vague crush, she is genuinely invested in their wellbeing. It was nice to see how in these turbulent times, her steadiness was something that was able to ground others. She provided genuine comfort to characters.

I did really enjoy getting to know these characters. The villains are fun too, I cheer whenever they show up. I really liked how each route fleshed out the story, helping us learn more about the characters and the mysteries happening. Each of the villains also gets highlighted in different routes, so you learn more about them as well. The main thing bringing the rating down is the repetitiveness and the slightly exasperating MC in some routes. Otherwise, Hakuoki Winds is pretty good.
