The long and short of my opinion is yes, and no. I played Hakuoki: Memories of the Shinsengumi on the 3DS years ago and was so ecstatic so see it revamped. This game is incredible, period, if you like a lot of story and depths behind that story. They did a fantastic job on the detail they put into the politics surrounding the time period this game takes place in. My only complaint was for some reason the English translation for Kyoto Winds/Edo Blossoms isn't the same as the 3DS variant and they made characters like Okita, Kazama, and Harada's dialogue a LOT more crude. Throwing in curse words in certain contexts that I felt hindered the experience rather than amplified it. Everytime Okita said "Stop having a bitch fit" left a bad taste in my mouth when in the 3DS version he was a lot more casual saying things like "There's no reason to get so worked up." While technically yes, they both have the same meaning, one just settles better than the other. 
The only one who truly cursed the most in the original translation was Hijikata, and I sort of wish they kept that going in this one too. 
Don't even get me started on how they disgraced Kazama's dialogue in a similar manner. While yes, his character is supposed to be demeaning in some routes, they gave him the tongue of a lowly sailor versus the eloquent speech of a respected head of a prosperous Demon clan in this particular translation. In the 3DS while he spoke in a derogatory manner it was much more graceful, akin to Sanan's manner of phrasing things, one can easily insult another without the need of constant cursing. This translator was just particularly fond of easy insults like "Bitch" to portray Kazama's angst. A direct example pulled from the game would be the Japanese term ばんけん (banken; in romanji) which directly translates to "Watchdog", instead of putting watchdog in the text they translated it as "Little bitch" which I feel pulls away from the fact that he was insulting the route's love Interest as nothing more than a watchdog for his Bride-to-be. Rather than directly insulting him for the sake of insulting. Yes Kazama has a negative outlook on human's as a species, but no he doesn't constantly curse at them every time he sees them. He just treats them like ants he can't be bothered with.  

The translator probably just did the easiest way of portraying the emotions with similar English phrases, over translating it word for word directly. Which I'm thankful for, but it also feels like a shame. 
I get that "Puppet for the Shinsengumi" and "Dog for the Shinsengumi" are in all technicality the same meaning. But if they very clearly said dog, why not just put dog instead of puppet? Does that make sense?

Other than that, everything about Kyoto Winds, and Edo Blossom are amazing. The sound track is incredible, I hum the title screen song all the time. The CGs are really nice, although some of them you can tell weren't created by the original artist, they still did justice to the game. And the story line is good about wrapping up lose ends (when you play both Kyoto Winds and Edo Blossom since KW is the first half and EB is the second half of one entire full route per character. 

Not sure if anyone actually reads reviews like this but those are my two cents!

In all my years as a strong member of the gaming community, I have never really been a fan of Visual Novels. No matter how much I tried, I never quite got the "Yeah, this could be my thing" stage. So, I was really surprised when 'Hakuoki: Kyoto Winds' immediately caught my eye during the Steam summer sale. I started to think that maybe I should give them another try. I did and I do not regret it.

[table]    
    [tr]
        [td][u]Story[/u][/td]
        [td]The story of 'Hakuoki: Kyoto Winds' takes place in Japan during the late shogunate period in the 19th century and shows the events before 'Hakuoki: Edo Blossoms'. We start the game playing the young gal Chizuru Yukimura, the daughter of a prestigious doctor named Kodo Yukimura. When Chizuru was younger, Kodo embarked on a secretive journey to Kyoto and disappeared. We start to sense that something is wrong, so we decide to leave our hometown of Edo and head to Kyoto, dressed as boys to be less of a target for ronin (rogue samurai), hoping to find answers to the questions that are circulating through our minds.

The story is distributed over five chapters. We experience the story in several chronological time frames that build upon one another.[/td]
    [/tr]
    [tr]
        [td][u]Characters[/u][/td]
        [td]I limit myself here to the protagonist and the six main characters. I'll also include my personal rating for each character's route, which will be based on my subjective romance factor, but I won't include any biographical information to prevent spoilers.

[u]Chizuru Yukimura[/u]
Before I start with the rest of the characters, I have to begin with the one we play as, and which bothers me the most: Chizuru. She is a well-mannered, polite, caring, shy, yet fearless young girl. 
Although I was able to identify with some of her character traits, there were still a few things that were nagging at me. I'm aware of the fact that Chizuru is very young when the story starts, but especially at the end of the game, I got very frustrated by her often naive mindset and almost impulsive behaviour. Sometimes it made me very angry that the player didn't get the opportunity to have more impact on her, like training her, so we can be a part of the action instead of only acting in the background. I don't dislike her character, I just think that her potential is completely wasted.

[u]Toshizo Hijikata[/u]
Toshizo is the vice-commander of the Shinsengumi and is based on the real [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hijikata_Toshizō] Hijikata Toshizō [/url]. He is strict, disciplined, but also thoughtful and mature. He puts the Shinsengumi over everything, including such things as honour. Starting Hijikata's route, I had high expectations. As we play his route, we get a glance of what is behind his hard shell and he definitely has his moments, but I still have rather mixed feelings about his ending. I like him as a character and I can see him and Chizuru growing closer in Edo Blossoms, but in this part of the game series, his route is unfortunately not one of my favourites.
Personal rating: [6.5/10] 

[u]Souji Okita[/u]
Souji is the captain of the 1st division in the Shinsengumi and is based on the real [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okita_Sōji] Okita Sōji [/url]. He's a charming character with rather sadistic and sarcastic character traits. He likes to tease, but he is also very loyal, especially towards Kondou, the commander, who is his role model. As we follow Okita's route, we find out that he can also be quite sensitive, almost impulsive. I really liked Okita's route. I had a lot of empathy with him, but I ended up having the same feelings that I had in Hijikata's ending.
Personal rating: [6.5/10] 

[u]Saito Hajime[/u]
Saito is the captain of the 3rd division in the Shinsengumi and is based on the real [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saitō_Hajime] Saitō Hajime [/url]. Saito is very quiet and loyal. He obeys Hijikata's orders without blinking, which makes him look a bit cold and emotionless in the beginning, although playing his route, we find out that he cares a lot about those he holds dear. His route is one of my favourites, because he made me, the player, feel less weak and powerless. That, in combination with his adorable characters, makes his route really enjoyable. 
Personal rating: [8.5/10] 

[u]Heisuke Toudou[/u]
Heisuke is the captain of the 8th division in the Shinsengumi and is based on the real [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tōdō_Heisuke] Tōdō Heisuke [/url]. Toudou is a cheerful young lad, and close to Yukimura's age. He's small, thin, loud and more of a boy than a man. When I started his route, I didn't have any expectations. I had the impression that he's too extroverted, too boyish and impulsive. But once I started his route, I started to like Toudou. Unexpectedly, his route from all the main characters was my absolute favourite.
Personal rating: [9/10] 

[u]Sanosuke Harada[/u]
Harada is the captain of the 10th division in the Shinsengumi and is based on the real [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harada_Sanosuke] Harada Sanosuke [/url]. »He spends a lot of time saying frightening things, but he is very genuine and warm.« - Chizuru (Chapter one). I think this quote is the best way to describe Harada. I liked Harada as a character a lot and I enjoyed playing his route, but I unfortunately ended up thinking that Yukimura and Sanosuke don't really fit together. Harada is a person who desperately wants to protect his lady, but as the unrequited love ending emphasizes again, Chizuru is not like ordinary girls. Sano can't protect her the way he wants to, which seems to frustrate him. Harada is great, but maybe not the best spouse for Chizuru.
Personal rating: [6/10] 
 
[u]Shinpachi Nagakura[/u]
Shinpachi is the captain of the 2nd division in the Shinsengumi and is based on the real [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagakura_Shinpachi] Nagakura Shinpachi [/url]. Shin is like a bison: His appearance is intimidating, but his nature is warm and cheerful. Before playing his story, I often assumed that Shin was unintelligent rather than brainy, and more focused on fighting than thinking. That's why I had low expectations when starting his path. But after experiencing his route, I was positively surprised to find out that Nagakura is not as carefree as he seems. I liked his story path, but I never really considered him as a potential love interest, but rather as a brother-like friend.
Personal rating: [4.5/10]

Short rating for the rest of the characters routes (due to the lack of space, I unfortunately couldn't include the detailed descriptions):
[u]Sanan[/u]: [2/10]
[u]Yamazaki[/u]: [9.5/10]
[u]Iba[/u]: [4/10]
[u]Souma[/u]: [6.5/10] 
[u]Sakamoto[/u]: [6/10]
[u]Kazama[/u]: [5/10][/td]
    [/tr]
    [tr]
        [td][u]Visual style, sounds and music[/u][/td]
        [td]What I like the most about this game, next to characters and story, is the visual art style. I can see the love and passion that was put into every CG, every background and every character. Eyes and mouth animations, sounds and music give the game more atmospheric depth. The music is not overwhelming, but it does add to the atmosphere.[/td]
    [/tr]
[td][u]Conclusion[/u][/td]
        [td]Overall, I can say that 'Hakuoki: Kyoto Winds' left me with a good impression. Despite some exceptions, I grew fond of the characters and as someone who likes history, I enjoyed getting a deeper insight into Japan during the 19th century. Unfortunately, I didn't know that this was the first half of the Hakuoki series when I started playing, which led to me being disappointed sometimes due to the lack of romance in some routes, even though it's promoted as a romance game. But they made me curious about what is to come in the next half and I think playing this and seeing the relationships of the characters develop might improve the game experience for Edo Blossoms.[/td]

[b]Why "romancing 12 men" seems like the wrong way to describe this:[/b]
I expected the romance to be woven within this story, in EVERY route. But, half of the routes don't have anything I'd call a love story in them. Although I suppose you could look at the duty and honor of a samurai as romantic.

Without spoilers I'll explain what I mean because I was a bit shocked honestly. Each route is written to fit the personality of the male love interest. The protagonist is just kinda along for the ride.

Flirty and cute and feel like the beginning of a dark fantasy based romance:
-Sakamoto & Hachiro Iba

Iba's is probably my favorite and the smoothest love journey for our MC.

Cutesy with subtle flirtations and romance woven around duty, honor, and sacrifice:
-Harada, Souma, & Heisuke

Sweet & shocking, developing into an intense friendship that made me want to cry:
-Souji

The mysterious guy chasing you trope, adding drama and suspense
-Kazama

"Sister zoned" or "that girl that just won't stop following me around":
Sanaan, Hijikata, Saito, Kamazaki & Nagakura

While there were many openings to slip in some romantic lines or scenes, all 5 focused more on the Shinsengumi, duty and honor as a samurai, the civil unrest, and ultimately, the brutality of war. 

As you can see, I did spend 100 hours reading and re-reading because it's a really fun read. Just don't have high expectations for the romance in each route. There is absolutely none in some of them. I only managed to do one bad ending though. I enjoyed the good endings far too much.

I should start off with saying that Kyoto Winds is only the first part of this remake of Hakuoki and is essentially only half a game. That being said, there's enough content there to last you a good 40 hours, with a lot of new routes that weren't in the original game.

Hakuoki is an Otome that takes place in the Tokugawa period as certain events lead to the main character staying with the famous Shinsengumi. Nearly all Shinsengumi members as well as most in-game events are based on real-life, which will teach you a lot about Japanese history.

As with most visual novels you start on a common route and choices made will lead you on different paths favouring different characters. Let me say this though: if you're just looking to romance handsome guys, this is the wrong half of the game to play. Kyoto Winds focuses on getting to know each character and building your friendship with them but it doesn't bloom into a romance until the second game called Edo Blossoms. That doesn't mean it's boring though, as each character has their own unique personality, story and background.

The production quality of the game is pretty good, with beautiful graphics, animated lip sync, great voice acting and a very nice OST. My playthroughs were super smooth on the SteamDeck with only a few minor spelling mistakes to note, and it was a great alternative to the Vita never having sales anymore.

Despite only being half a game, this is a solid visual novel and I'm looking forward to the second part. These games are pretty cheap on Steam and on sale a lot, so having to buy two games to get the full story shouldn't be an issue to anyone a fan of Otome games.

I'm likely going to revisit this review once I finish the game, however, it has been suggested that I split up the game because of how long it can be if you listen to all the voiced dialogue and go through every route, both of which I (intend to) do. So, here I am, 5 endings out of 30, and 55 hours with only two men romanced, though I wouldn't really call it romancing. Even put mildly, even considering the time period, this specific game (Kyoto Winds) is more of friendship building than romance building, and you have to have an appreciation for the story more than looking to romance some hot guys. I came into the game understanding this, after reading reviews that said the romance is in Edo Blossoms, I can completely confirm this.

Kyoto Winds is, in essence, the very long common route to Edo Blossoms, where sometimes the MC might figure out she has some sort of feelings towards a LI, but she's not entirely sure what those feelings are, if they exist at all, and then the ending practically says: To Be Continued. Does that make the game bad? No. I don't think so. Unless your aim is simply to kiss the dude, then you're going to be sorely out of luck in that regard.

What's good, bad, and in-between about this game?

Good: Several branching stories and paths. I feel like my choices actually matter. Different options lead to different revelations so repeated play throughs (and there will be many since there are 12 LIs) doesn't (yet) feel like a chore. Skip feature for read text, so when you do eventually know everything, you don't have to slog through 10 hours of the same story that you didn't find interesting. Saying that, there isn't much that I didn't find interesting. I reread every bit. Service Record section in the main menu, allowing you to pick up at a specific chapter instead of starting all over. Lovely art. Music I didn't get tired of hearing. Even considering the mystical aspects of this historical fiction, the stories were realistic and people were seriously injured or even died. I tend to enjoy when mortality is not only possible, but likely and the heroes (whether it be MC or LIs) don't have plot armor.

Bad: It really bothered me the amount of the game where there was no BGM. I understand stopping it for dramatic purposes, but sometimes it was simply gone for no reason, and for an extended period of time. And the scenes where they looped the same 2 seconds of background chatter to give the impression of busy areas, super annoying. MC is predominantly helpless. If you want a damsel in distress, this is perfect. Flimsy excuses for the MC's personality, both for flaws and strengths; it simply makes little sense for why she is the way she is and instead of just saying that's the character they input illogical correlations for causation. MC doesn't grow, really. The game takes place over 4 years and she's practically the same person from beginning to end.

In-between: MC is self-aware enough to acknowledge how useless, unintelligent, and inexperienced she is without dwelling on it, so it doesn't turn into a pity-party, nor spur any sort of fervent tasks to be a better person. Translation. It isn't that it is poorly translated, it's that the language is extremely modernized and Americanized, so certain ideas aren't expressed in a clear manner unless you know about Japanese culture and the Japanese vocabulary associated with those ideas that you so happen to pick up on through the verbal dialogue and not the written text. I don't see how it would be possible to get the route you're aiming for without a guide, if you are the type to aim for certain LIs. I tend to play and see where it takes me, but eventually I'll want to go down everyone's path, and I'm not sure I'll be able to without much trial and error due to the amount of choices that are either removed or changed based on previous choices.

TL;DR: It's really not a bad game, and I dare even say it is a GOOD game as long as you don't go in with expectations of steamy, romantic stories, light-hearted fluff, or men solely interested in the MC, since they all have their own agenda and MC is pretty much along for the ride.

It took me a while, but I finally completed [i]Hakuouki: Kyoto Winds [/i]last week. 

Before commenting on the game at length, I should mention a few things:

[olist]

[*]I've played the original version (specifically, the Android port). This review represents my best efforts to provide insight into my experience playing [i]Kyoto Winds[/i] with as little bias as possible.
[*]I have also made an effort to avoid spoilers. 
[*] I played [i]Kyoto Winds[/i] in English, so my remarks on its writing concern the English translation, not the Japanese original or the Chinese translation.
[/olist]

This version of [i]Hakuouki[/i] is a partial remake of the original game, which has seen a few re-releases under different titles and with slightly different extra content (think side stories). It is also only one half of the story: the amount of new content, including animated character sprites, apparently made it necessary for the remaster to be released as two games. I recently learned that the second game will be released for the Vita in 2018, so hopefully that means we'll get a Steam release and needn't worry about investing time and money in an incomplete story.

[i]Hakuouki: Kyoto Winds[/i] is set in Japan during the late Edo era, a time of political and cultural upheaval for the country. The protagonist, Chizuru Yukimura, finds herself caught in the middle of it when she comes to Kyoto looking for her missing father. (Players of the game can change her first name if they wish; I will refer to the protagonist as Chizuru for my review.)

I've always liked Chizuru, but I was happy to see her given a more active role. Her experience in medicine is modest, but the remake gives it much more importance. Included in the new material are scenes (on and off the battlefield) which more clearly demonstrate her courage and stubbornness. 

Because [i]Hakuouki[/i] is an [i]otome[/i] game—that is, a romance game with male love interests, a female protagonist, and a primarily female player demographic—the story is divided into routes by character. In addition to a common route wherein Chizuru remains romantically unattached, there are twelve character routes. In general, the game makes it easy to determine which choices are linked to which character(s). There's also a “romance up” indicator that appears when a choice made increases a character's affection for Chizuru. It can be turned off if desired. (Some choices won't display this indicator but may increase affection.)

Each character's route has a happy end, an unrequited love end, and a bad end. Once a route is cleared, it can be easily replayed by chapter from the main menu, with affection set to “high” or “low.” This feature makes it easy to get the less-than-happy ends, though the player could stumble into one if a chosen character's affection level isn't high enough.

The bulk of my review, however, focuses on the quality of the game's writing, which varies wildly and tends to be worse where the story includes new material. I saw many typos, including punctuation errors, missing words and extra words, and sometimes incomplete sentences! I believe an update has fixed at least some of the incompleteness—I had to speed through portions of the game to re-register them as read after an update—but I'll have to replay a route or two to confirm my assertion. I remember Sannan's route looked especially sloppy.

The main problem plaguing [i]Hakuouki: Kyoto Winds[/i]'s English translation is an unfortunate misunderstanding of English grammar. I say this not to be rude; even as a native speaker I understand how confusing and irregular English grammar can be. I was just surprised since the translation of the original had far fewer issues, especially regarding tenses. (There seems to be confusion about when to use simple past versus past perfect.)

Other problems relate to word choice. Sometimes, when reading a bit of text, I saw words that I knew weren't used correctly, either because of homophone problems (the example I can remember is past and passed), or because of other mistaken definitions (unrelated to trouble with similar-sounding words). The last nit I have to pick regarding word choice just relates to text that was technically accurate, but a word used made it rather stiff and unnatural-sounding. For example, “I tried to run” flows better than “I attempted to run.”

It's difficult for me to summarize these issues in a review that's meant to be short (though I do have a few explanatory screenshots uploaded), especially since there are other minor quibbles I wish I had time to discuss. Those playing the game, however, should see what I mean. It's a damn shame, because [i]Hakuouki[/i] is full of beautiful art and music, and the characters are well acted. I'm sure if many dozens of literary-minded fans got together in a room, they could help correct these problems. I know I'd happily contribute.

Despite the flawed localization, [i]Hakuouki: Kyoto Winds[/i] is a moving experience filled with endearing characters, and earns my recommendation. It may be classified as a romance game, but I believe there's something in it for everyone to enjoy. Anybody interested in reading a coming-of-age story mixed with elements of wartime drama, political change, and a dash of the supernatural should consider it.

Only finished 8/12 routes as of this writing, but so far it's definitely worth it! Initially, I was skeptical on whether I would like it, hence, I bought it on a sale. I'm  not really a fan of history-heavy games, and the art really felt dated at first. However, the game's plot and structure were enough to keep me intrigued, and Hakuoki lived up to its hype as a classic of the otome genre. Contrast this with Ozmafia, a game whose art style captivated me, but lost me with its messy storytelling and its inability to engage with the readers. Oh, and all the love interests have their own unique charms, so there's bound to be one for everybody.

There have been some complaints over its translation, especially when compared to the original PSP version, but this didn't really bother me, having not played that version. The way the plot was chopped between this and Edo Blossoms may seem weird, but it actually made sense.

I am currently only a third of the way through completing this game, but feel I can give a solid recommendation based on what I have played so far. 

Pros: 
- replay value is high - I'm at 40 hours, and feel like there's a lot I haven't discovered, and characters I haven't really gotten to know because they're locked away in another route.
- gorgeous game - the visual and aural design of the game creates a fluid, dynamic experience. The battle scenes are actually exciting to watch, even with everyone being 2D figures. 
- storytelling - YMMV, depending on taste, but I found the storytelling extremely compelling. I was invested in the characters, I wanted them to succeed, and I was happy that the choices I made affected not only what happend to the MC, but affected the events in the timeline as well. That's not always the case with otome, but good otome changes the universe. 
- humor/drama balance - there's a lot of tragedy, but a lot of humor. I thought the balance was well done here. Even if you're not on a particularly positive route (there are some that are more depressing than others), there are moments you can't avoid that lighten the mood. We get to laugh with these characters as well as grieve with them.

Cons:
- if you don't like history, you might find this a bit dry. I personally loved that they connected the game to real historical events. 
- there is some repetition in the main events of the story. Fortunately, the game allows you a way to skip through those bits, or you can do what I do and give your brain a rest before returning. For my personal experience, I have been able to see the scenes differently depending on what else I have experienced in the playthrough I'm on.
- incomplete - this game gives an incomplete experience. I do think it is necessary to play Edo Blossoms and continue the story directly after. Kyoto Winds will not give you a resolution, but I don't think I would have been connected to the characters in Edo Blossoms nearly as much if I hadn't played Kyoto Winds first.

I do recommend this game, with the caveat that you should follow it up with Edo Blososms, and give yourself time to sink into it. For those who love a little bit of historical fiction, this should be right up your alley.

*I will include some historical facts in this review. I will put them in spoiler tag.

[b]ABOUT HAKUOUKI: [/b] It is a long-running (& successful) otome franchise in Japan, and also one of the most famous names in this genre (which is probably the reason why you're here too). I've heard about it since forever, but due to mixed reviews, I never actually put my hand on it. Not gonna lie, I felt like this game is already pretty out-of-date. But since it is kinda a big name in the industry, I bought it just thinking "well it doesn't hurt if it sucks, I just want the experience." I haven't finished every route, but I have played all the 'iconic' one and a few of new ones.

[b]PLOT: [/b] This is the part 1 of the full story, you need to buy Edo Blossom to reach the ending of each route. I believe a big background research into the era will help you enjoy the story better, it also explains a lot of characters' behaviour in the game. The plot for this part revolves mainly around the heroine joining Shinsengumi in their daily life and began to understand them better. If you want a quick summary: This story sets in the Bakumatsu era, an era that brought massive change to Japan. [spoiler] Japan isn't doing good. They are standing in front of the danger of being colonised by Western countries. The current government system was in-name ruled by both Tokugawa shogunate (holds actual power) and the Emperor (the puppet). At the time, the shogunate system was already really rotten and about to collapse, and the new Emperor Meiji seized power (he just took over his power again, because it's supposed be him in power anyway). This change is extremely important in Japan history, 'cause thanks to the Meiji Restoration, Japan is now steps ahead in term of development in compare to other Asian countries. So IMO, in this game, you basically sides with stubborn people who can't accept a necessary change to the system. Thus this makes the Shinsengumi no hero. The great thing is, I believe there are people in the cast who fully aware that changes must be done, but can't do otherwise because of their commitment. So if you play the game and know the history, think about why a character did the thing they did - or did the way they did, you will get a much much deeper understanding about them. [/spoiler] The story highlights on the conflict between two forces - shogunate force (those who support the current system, Shinsengumi for example) and the nationalists (those who wish a new system, a new Japan). If you understand the history here (aka the situation of Japan), it will help explaining a lot of decisions made by the cast, which makes the depth of a character. I have seen reviews where they said some characters had no depth, or 'was losing his mind when he decided it' etc. but I think it's just because they don't really understand the setting of the game. Personally I'm a history nerd so it's up to you to decide not to dig it or not, since history is not everyone's piece of cake. But a background will enhance your experience, no doubt. The game also taught me a lot of new historical terms too, so that's a plus to me.

I do not typically enjoy otome games (no judgment against those who do, just my personal preferences), but I unexpectedly love this game. I guess I'm a bit of a Shinsengumi fan (having grown up watching a ton of historical dramas and been primed for this kind of thing by virtue of ethnicity/cultural background, probably), so that could be a large part of it, but besides that, I was also kind of relieved that the character relationships aren't so much the kind of cheesy "romance" I expected from otome (at least based on what I've seen in passing) but are refreshingly complex and not necessarily even overtly romantic. I can't remember the last time I felt so fondly toward a cast of fictional characters, and RPGs are my bread and butter. (Okay, well, other than the protagonist, who tends to be groan-inducingly stupid and helpless most of the time.) The events surrounding Shinsengumi were already well tread ground to me when I played this game, but Hakuoki's supernatural spin and the outstanding fictionalized portrayals of the characters (loosely based on historical figures) are more than enough to make this game more than yet another take on the Shinsengumi mythos.

Also, the translation is generally pretty excellent. There are definitely numerous parts where understanding the fully voiced Japanese dialogue greatly enhanced my experience of a scene (mostly more subtle nuances that aren't reflected in the English translation), but all in all, I think the English translation captures the spirit of the dialogue well. I do wish the translators didn't throw in needless expletives, though. They often aren't actually in the original dialogue. Regardless, great voice acting, art, and writing throughout.

In short, I fully recommend this game to folks who like story-/character-driven games and don't mind reading or a little gore (not gratuitous), even if, like me, you don't usually go for visual novels or otome games.

I've been a VN enthusiast for awhile now and this game and its sequel caught my eye in a recent sale. I was thinking, "Hmm, I want some romance, this looks good." I did indeed get some flashes of romance, though relatively subtle and subdued, in the lengthy and complex story. But I was soon completely caught in the world and the time and the turmoil it was set in. Immediately arrested by the setting and conflicts, though they were in another country centuries ago on the other side of the world, I started researching them on the side as I made my way through the story. I found the real historical bones of it very easy to pick out from the flights of fancy that make it a historical fantasy. To be honest, I'd rather have less apparent romance in a story where the setting, conflicts, all the characters and their relationships with each other are so fleshed out as this one, because it makes the romance more poignant and believable when you do get a glimmer or foreshadowing of it. I hear the second part of the game, Edo Blossoms, has the actual romance parts of the stories, and it feels like it will be so much more rewarding after the work to weave the friendship in Kyoto Winds. 

The parts of a visual novel that will make it or kill it are the art and the writing. I've given up playing VNs that were well written but had horrible art, and given up on others that had lovely art but poor writing. Either or both factors failing can make a game unbearable. Kyoto Winds has gorgeous art in the soft organic backgrounds, expressive sprites, and immersive CGs. And powerful writing where all the characters feel interconnected to each other and you get a multifaceted perspective on them in the different stories. They feel internally consistent though you get constantly varying angles on them, and they're mirroring the greater stresses Japan was going through at the time. This is one reason so many different things about the story stayed with me, because the game explained so well why different people were in the position they were in or feeling what they were feeling. 

Now we come to the next important part of a VN if it's an otome and has a heroine - the heroine herself. I think a game can still work if the writing is patchy here or leaves the player to imagine more details, because of the self-insert nature. However I feel that Chizuru is a wonderful heroine. Some have interpreted her as simply weak, or feeble. I like how she doesn't have remarkable fighting skills, but knows basic self defense and strives to learn more about that too. I like that she cooks and cleans a lot in the situation she is in and takes pleasure in it. And while I like all of this and it seems realistic, I love that while she has to dress as a boy she doesn't lose her connection to feminine things or her own grace and spirit. And at some points in the game where she makes a risky decision, or stands up to someone, or asks the man she loves a hard question, it forces me at that point in the story to ask, would I have that same courage? I love when a story pushes me to do that with the protagonist I'm fusing with. 

The love interests themselves were fascinating to pursue, and question why I felt drawn to them or not. It stands out to me that this game has twelve different men and it doesn't ever feel like it's repeating itself. I do think it would be interesting if Princess Sen and her beautiful bodyguard were also love interests as well, however I don't know enough about the culture then in the 1860s to know how that would be perceived or how an LGBT story would be written. So I understand if they wanted to focus on the men (I also just really enjoy Sen's role as my gal pal in the story, bc I really need one.)  

First and foremost, I fell hopelessly in love with Sanan and Iba (which, if you have played the game, you will laugh because their personalities are hysterically different), but Sanan's story tore and claimed my heart the most which is saying a lot because a lot of the stories did that to me, and Iba is just sweet and lovely. I also really loved quiet Saito as well. Sakamoto's charismatic, gregarious, progressive character was charming too. Hijikata's route was almost not romantic if at all, but I hear his story gets *really* romantic in the sequel, so I'll be waiting for that. The men I weren't drawn to as much personally were still very engaging characters and I still enjoyed reading their stories, because they felt just as real as my favorites. All in all none of it was in the least a waste of time. 

*Note, it's recommended to play Kazama last because of story reveals and impact in the game, I didn't quite want to play him last bc he wasn't my most favorite (he did get some depth in his story thankfully, and Chizuru gets some really exciting growth with her character too.). However I did play him next to last and can confirm that was a good decision. So last or next to last for him I would say.

[h1]TL;DR:[/h1] An absolute classic for a reason, with a surprising array of selection in love interests... but not for everyone. Probably especially new readers to the genre. (It's a bit heavy for people going into it lightly.) On the other hand - it may be a great introductory title for history lovers or people not usually into otome. (For example - straight guys who want to branch out into the stories otome have to offer without diving into the deep end.)

---

[h1]Overall Impression:[/h1]  The story is heavily based on actual Japanese history. Part one (Kyoto Winds) is primarily about the history and getting to know the different men involved with the shinsengumi and surrounding historical figures and events. The heroine and her budding romance is barely touched upon in Kyoto Winds, and even in Edo Blossoms, is not as romance-heavy as many other otome titles. 

This makes a great gateway otome for people not particularly interested in romance, but can be very dry for people who aren't interested in history or slow-moving plots. It's one of my favorites and not just because it was one of my very first otome. That said - with 12 love interests, it can be an absolute chore to get all the endings if you're trying to do it back-to-back, so be prepared for that.


[h1]Content:[/h1]  The most important warning to keep in mind is that there is a lot of violence and death - some of it historical and some of it purely fictional. Some of it can be absolutely gut-wrenching, though not necessarily as over-the-top traumatic as some VN bad ends can be. There is some implication of sexual violence and some even threatened - but nothing is really done "on screen", so it shouldn't be an issue for many readers.

The story also leans towards more historical accurate in terms of womens roles. That is to say - don't expect the heroine to be treated like a modern woman. It would be difficult to say that she is ever treated fully as an equal by most of the characters, but at the very least most of them do respect her for her strengths and appreciate her as a person.


[h1]Translation/Editing/Glitches:[/h1]  There is little by way of translation error or awkwardness, though some typos in a story of this size are inevitable. There were, however, a couple of glitches. IIRC, it was mostly during transitions, so not a big deal - just worth mentioning.


[h1]Art/Character Design:[/h1]  The skill of the artwork is self-evident from the screenshots. Some of the character designs and CGs are some of my favorite in my otome library. I felt like the artist could have been pushed more as I know they're capable, but the only thing I actually find disappointing is a certain CG that most routes get that displays a moment of deepening intimacy between the heroine and love interest. I hate having to gather all 3+ variations of it.


[h1]The Heroine:[/h1]  She's probably not going to be anyone's [i]favorite[/i] otome heroine. But I do like her quite a bit. Many readers might find her too bland or passive - but she's just not their speed. Being passive and willing to adapt is not a bad thing at all. [b]This isn't her story[/b]. She is a witness to the story of the shinsengumi and at best, supports them to the bitter end. Many readers who wish to vicariously live out their fantasies of being a kick-ass protagonist themselves won't like that. And that's fine! But Chizuru isn't that heroine. If that isn't for you, consider saving this for when you're in a mood where you don't mind being swept away in someone else's story. Many of the love interests (IMHO) are fully worth it, even if you can't identify with Chizuru herself.

(I [i]do[/i] wish that either her sword was never part of the story at all or she was at least good enough with it to justify having it. It's frustrating to be told that she was pretty good with a sword and then in practice, be useless. I know this was to underscore how amazing the love interests are, but it was at the expense of undermining Chizuru.)


[h1]The Love Interests:[/h1]  There... are so many, I won't go over them individually because reviews just don't give that much space. But I will say that this is one otome where I like most of the LIs. And with a full dozen to choose from, you'll probably find at least one you like. Character types I generally don't like proved they were worth reading. Even the character whose story I liked least (Shinpachi - green bandana) had an ending that I think isn't an exaggeration to say haunts me. I find myself thinking of it every so often as I wonder what the heroine's life was like after the last word written.

I will say that the slow burn on some of the characters can be frustrating if you're just out for a quick "hot boys" story. These are passionate, driven men. These men had goals in life before the heroine showed up in it - and sometimes, those goals run directly in conflict with their feelings for her, so it makes sense for them to take awhile to fall in love - or at least show they have. 


[h1]Story:[/h1]  History of the Shinsengumi 101. Also supernatural stuff to give the heroine something to do in the story other than gawk at the men and do housekeeping - and, y'know, explain how their stories continue after the point where in history they'd die, I suppose. 


[h1]In closing...[/h1]  As I've said before - it's a classic for a reason. As long as you're willing to at least skim over the history section (none of the choices you make are going to quiz you on the history, so by all means, skim if you need to - there's no shame in that even if you do miss out on some of the context of their personal storylines), it's an amazing title for you to pick up.

**Also - you probably don't need the DLCs - at least not at full price. There are only twelve stories (six in Kyoto Winds and six in Edo Blossoms) that are only a couple hundred words each. I was very disappointed.

[h1] History but Sexy [/h1]
First thing is first. This is the first part of a two part game. This is a slow burn romance where you get history and get to know your fellah over the course of a few years. I have played EVERY ending.

Your character is Yukimura Chizuru (or whatever name you give her) and she basically exists for self insert purposes. Honestly, I wish she could do cooler stuff given her heritage. But her behavior generally depends on which route she's in. I do enjoy that she is quite kind. A bit of an airhead at times and you wanna spell things out for her, but she is likable. Not that active, but she does have her goals/mission.

The art is absolutely beautiful. I fell in love with the style. It is a history heavy game, especially part one setting you up for part two. This game is pretty historically accurate, which I found enjoyable. That being said, this is about the rise of a civil war so prepare for some heartbreak. Those of you that liked Nightshade will enjoy this as I think it was actually better.

Characters/Romance style: They're all pretty different. I will block out anything I deem spoiler-y but mostly I'm describing the romance.

Toshizo Hijikata: "Canon." He has the prettiest hair. This romance felt more like you exist as a Greek chorus to watch events unfold since he is a prominent figure of the war. It gets sweeter towards the end.

Souji Okita: I found this to be the most believable route with life just throwing crap his way and Souji dealing with it the best he could. Smart mouth tsundere type. It had its sweet moments. Take a shot for every time Okita says he'll kill you and you'll have alcohol poisoning by the end of this game. That being said, I loved this brat.

Heisuke Toudou: Hilarious start. It's really quite cute as the characters fall for each other. I enjoyed that this character was immediately warm to Chizuru, very much like an excited puppy. This one was a pretty natural progression of feelings that's actually visible in the story.

Sanosuke Harade: MC is SO much stronger in this. There's a mutual sort of respect between the two characters. Sanosuke respects her strength, and even though he's a gentleman trying to protect her, he'll listen to her. Friends to lovers sort of feel.

Shinpachi: F this romance. I'm warning you, this one feels like an older brother.

Hajime Saito: Typical shy guy. Lots of cute moments. There's way more to him and Chizuru helps Saito become more.

Susumu Yamazaki: This guy totally surprised me. Not what I expected at all. Really sweet romance and this character has the potential to become a stronger character because of Chizuru. She has more of a presence in this one because of their [spoiler] similar medical background in healing and she contributes alongside him [/spoiler].

Hachiro Iba: Marry me. Childhood friends trope. Sometimes it is so painfully obvious you want to take Chizuru to the side and say very slowly, "He likes you." He respects Chizuru's desires over what he thinks is best. It's refreshing to have a character who openly expresses their feelings.

Chikage Kazama: I could listen to this man talk for hours. Holy crap the voice actor sends ripples down your spine. My bae. The narrative makes it so Chizuru is out of the loop on a lot of war sh*t, however, the trade off is that Kazama is very dutiful in filling in the blanks about her demon heritage. I enjoyed this alone for learning about that, but he had to have the voice of a sex god so that was a plus. It feels like he's trying to meet you halfway.

Royuma Sakamoto: Eh. He's pretty. This romance is more through correspondence and picks up towards the end.

Kazue Souma: You don't meet this guy for like half of the game. This is more of a very slow growth sort of romance. You get the feeling towards the end that they both [spoiler] like each other but are too shy to do anything [/spoiler]. Nomura is hilarious.

Keisuke Sanan: Okay, he gets a bad rep. Found his route enjoyable but I have a thing for characters that have a dark side growing within them. *shakes fist at Dragon Age Inquisition* You can tell that that the protagonist becomes to Sanan [spoiler] his only source of light and she helps him retain his humanity [/spoiler]. Feels like a romance where the two people like each other but are afraid to cross that line, in Sanan's case it is because of duty.

If you want my opinion on each of the boys/dating routes:

Toshizo Hijikata
The father you always looked up to and admired, who rarely says they're proud of you without a backhanded comment. If you've got neglectful daddy issues, Hijikata's your man.

Souji Okita
He's the reason your mother would tell you "he's only mean because he likes you."
If you like being bullied, degraded, threatened with bodily harm, then heavily flirted with in a confusing mixed-message banter, Okita's more than happy to roast you.

Hajime Saito
Silent, sullen, a man of few words. He's the shy emo kid (even has his hair half in his face). If you want someone that is aloof, but then uncharacteristically dotes you, Saito will leave you on read and get back to you later.

Heisuke Toudou
Very much the "boyish charm" trope. Heisuke reminds me of that boisterous and rakous middle-school type romance. If you want an adventure (and maybe a headache from loud yelling and screaming), Toudou will drag you with him.

Sanosuke Harada
This is the one you take home to mom. He self admits to a colored past, but is one of those rare gems that isn't broken by their experiences and instead turns into someone amazing. He's confident, calm, compassionate, but also a realist, all at the same time. Excellent sense of humor and even more fun when drunk (personally, my ideal guy, 12/10). If you want a husband, marry Harada.

Shinpachi Nagakura
Meat head through-and-though. This is the guy that goes to the YMCA and dead lifts a 350lb rack just so he can slam it on the floor hard enough for all the women sculpting their asses on the elliptical machines to turn and look at him. If your idea of romance is babysitting a massive sack of childishly impulsive muscles, Nagakura would love to showboat for you.

Keisuke Sanan
Sanan is creppy from the very start. With an almost hissing pattern of speech, and those extra sharply squinted eyes, he gives me evil Orochimaru vibes. If you've ever wanted to date the school shooter, Sanan would be happy to tell you his body count.

Susumu Yamazaki
Ponytail mullet boy. The silent protector that lurks in the shadows. Despite being a ninja, he's not very edgey or broody, but rather even tempered and personable. Kind of plain in flavor, but still enjoyed it. If you want mayonaise flavored romance, pick Yamazaki.

Hachiro Iba
Literally a love-sick puppy (I mean, who hasn't heard the story of Hachi?). He can be charmingly forward, and also fiercely protective. If you call his name, I'm sure you'd see his tail wagging. If you want a really good boy, go for Iba.

Kazue Souma
Brown noser. Totally sucks up to the lead characters, and overall was simple-minded as far as character dynamics go. If you used to have a crush on the teacher's pet, date Souma.

Ryouma Sakamoto
As strait as a strait-shooter can get. Incredibly blunt, and to the point. He borders on that obnoxious machismo, but, he has a few moments where he humbles himself. If you want Japanese Johnny Bravo, go for Sakamoto.

Chikage Kazama
Typical "misunderstood bad boy." Says a few poetic things, but is still a deplorable sociopath. If you like guys who are mentally detached with agression issues, Kazama would be happy to kidnap you (repeatedly).

Well written, well drawn/animated, excellently voice acted, one of the best otomes I've played in a long, long time. If you're a completionist, you're going to get bang for your buck. I've gotten all of the "good" endings a few others besides and still have sunk ample time into it. Worth it!

'Kay. I'm gonna come right out and say this: Perhaps this isn't worth buying if you've already bought the game before, which, all things considered, is incredibly likely. It could be if you're interested in the new routes, but prepare to spend an incredibly short amount of time alone with whoever it is you're targeting as this is only the first half of the game, ending right at the route split. I don't think this is clarified anywhere and I was totally baffled by the "mixed" score when I first blindly bought this because I rush into things like an idiot and was focused entirely on SANAN ROUTE, but now I know! This is some MGS: Ground Zeroes shit right here, my dude. I'm still going to recommend this as it goes down way smoother than the original, but be warned that. Like. The rest of the story is very obviously missing. It ends abruptly right before things are getting interesting. EXTREMELY abruptly.

If you want the short version of my review, it's this: "Okay, cool! Nice. Where's the rest of it?"

Now for the long.

My memory is trash so please forgive me if my comparisons aren't right on the money, but I'm going to hold this up against my blearly, fragmented snapshots of my first encounter with this game.

Firstly, it's visually stunning at any resolution and the new soundtrack is great. (I particularly had a problem with the old title theme because it was the absolute most generic jidai-geki instrumental theme you could imagine. It makes sense, but gave me flashbacks to my grandma hogging our TV to watch samurai dramas.) It's slick and easier to listen to. I do have a problem with it, but this has more to do with audio mixing which I'll get to later.

Graphically, as I said, it's beautiful. The lip flaps can be distracting (and look a little off to me) but it's forgivable. The new text box is fantastic, the menus are fantastic, and if I had any complaint about them it'd be that the "warrior record" has such an insane amount of negative space that it's a little difficult to figure out what it even is at first glance. I get that the blossoming cherry-blossom tree in the background is an affection meter and can applaud the creativity, but... I feel like it could have been executed a little better.

The text seems like it's been heavily streamlined. The first time I played this game I had to stop every so often because it felt [i]incredibly[/i] dense for a VN, but this feels far lighter. It's still heavy on history, but there really is no way to take that out of the story. If you've already played you know what to expect. If you're a new player, to put it shortly, "you gon' learn." Literally. This could be a huge problem if you're mainly looking for fluff. Hakuoki is already notoriously light on fluffy moments--which are increased here--but this is still mainly a historical fantasy.

I'm going to be an oddball here and say that I like the new routes better than the original ones. I loved the original, but I wasn't really interested in any of the guys... except for inaccessable Sanan. Which is why I bought this to begin with! His focus here has just the right amount of cold, subdued menace I was expecting. Sanan, out of all of the new suitors, has the least amount of fluff which is interesting considering the global fluff increase this game underwent. (This is great for me, but if you're wanting to go in and melt Sanan's bitter heart then. Well... Sorry.)  Iba is your typical smiley caring childhood friend type who would never hurt a fly. IMO, the most interesting part of his route was the presence of Kanryusai Takeda, who is a shamelessly messy bitch who lives for drama. He's so monumentally jealous and scheming that it accidentally made him charming in my eyes. Souma is your very own kouhai who SCREAMS CONSTANTLY and was pretty forgettable to me aside from that. He's cute and REALLY LOUD, but... that's really it. The strongest of the new routes for me was Ryouma Sakamoto's, he's really fun and a welcome departure from all the heavy "HONOR" stuff constantly happening, so I went ahead and played his route again instead of finishing Yamazaki's so I could form an appropriate opinion on it. (Uh...)

Anyhow: Now for my biggest problem with this game aside from the second half being conspicuously missing. THE AUDIO MIXING. The mixing is all over the place, usually the voices in a VN are normalized, but here they're... not. They are OBVIOUSLY not. Shinpachi in particular is so incredibly, ear-bleedingly loud for no reason that I had to turn his voice down a whole lot and he was STILL loud. Other voices, like Iba's and Kazama's, are very soft, so they have to be turned all the way up. But when they raise their voices, it's still too much! (Souma in particular is a ride from hell since he has both of these problems bad: Being very soft and very loud at the same time. His shouts in particular are so loud that they have obvious artifacting. It's... not great.) The music was drowning out a lot of the softer voices, so I turned it down as far as I could while still hearing it, but it was still too loud. I turned it down a little more then it was nearly inaudible! I spent a huge amount of time fiddling with the mixing of various voices, sound effects, and the music. I got to near comfortable levels with the voices and effects, but the music is just doomed to being a faint whisper. I can't get it to play at a reasonable volume. 

All in all: If you're new to Hakuoki, don't want to buy a vita and don't mind waiting indefinitely for the second part to be localized, knock yourself out. This is a great rerelease in spite of all of its issues, but you definitely need to take them into account and carefully decide whether or not you're okay with them. Purchasing this game when it goes on sale is perhaps your best bet, to be perfectly honest!

I recommend this game because it has very strong points, and Hakuouki as a franchise is definitely worth it, but it has issues that really take away from the enjoyment.

[u]The issues[/u]
- Well it's only half of a game. I think it was a mistake to split the game in two, because in this first installment you are left with a lot of unresolved plot threads, unanswered questions, and an ending so open it doesn't feel like an ending at all. (Because it's not ; it's the middle of the story.)
- It's not an actual PC port. I'm glad to be able to play on PC, but the UI shows only the original commands and does not adapt to keyboard, mouse or controller. You have to figure out the controls yourself. If you play on fullscreen the image will probably be blurry because PC screen resolutions aren't supported. Play in windowed mode if you have this issue.
- While it's good to have an English version, the translation is terrible. Speech is overly interpreted (making it unnecessary vulgar and misogynistic) with a few sentences being complete inventions, some are just plain wrong (they mean the opposite of what is said), there are typos (missing letters, missing words, misspellings)... A lot of sentences don't feel very natural in English either.

[u]The good points[/u]
- The game is very good at making you feel emotions. Even just the prologue will make you nostalgic for a time a place you don't even know yet. Everything tugs at your heartstrings, from conflicting loyalties to reticent betrayals to tragically unbreakable friendships... I think it's the game's strongest point.
- The music is great, and its use greatly enhances the gameplay. The headquarters music will feel like home to you. The complete silence will impart how scary a scene is. Another stong point.
- The voice acting is amazing, with great voice actors <3
- The illustrations are beautiful, especially the CGs.
- Despite the high number of routes and several mandatory events, each story is very different and each character fulfills a different fantasy. There is definitely value in playing all the routes, even if a character does not interest you at first.
- The game teaches you an incredible amount of things about the bakumatsu and the Shinsengumi, which is nice if you don't know anything, and great if you're already a fan of either.

All in all more good points than bad, but be sure to play Edo Blossoms too in order to get the whole story !

I can hardly consider this part of the game an otome title, as all romance is kept for the second part, Edo Blossoms, but it's a very enjoyable read anyway. You're presented with the ability to build up bonds with one out of 12 available men, so that's still something!

- All characters are very different and it's interesting to see how they open up once they get closer to you.

- Soundtrack is really enjoyable.

Overall, I can say this is a great read, definitely worth a pick together with Edo Blossoms for the full experience.

[h1]For those who have never played Hakuouki, I offer a glowing review:[/h1]
[quote]If you have played a previous version of Hakuouki and just want to see what’s new in this release, I have a review on Edo Blossoms that discusses only the new content [url=https://steamcommunity.com/profiles/76561197995408661/recommended/733340]here[/url]. [/quote]
Firstly, this is an otome so the target audience is teenage girls, and the situations and story do reflect that, but the character development, theme, and historical focus seem more refined than a typical for-girls story, landing this in the josei category of literature. Secondly, though it promises romance, this is only the first half of a two-part game ending on a cliff-hanger; the romance doesn’t show up until the sequel, so be prepared to double the price tag. I’ve only played two visual novels like this—loved this one and hated the other—and being a bit older than the target demographic, I’m likely to offer a different view than others who are more experienced with the genre.

The voice acting, without exception, is superb. Every romanceable character is unique and interesting, though nearly all of them take some warming up to and are given plenty of room for character growth, and the story’s subtle characterization truly makes you want to learn and understand your potential love interest. However, these men are soldiers, and I think the game does a pretty good job of constantly reminding you that their priorities are soldiering and not wooing little girls—until the end (in Edo Blossoms) when everything starts going to pieces and the only one who can save the day is you! I really cannot express how excellent the story-telling is for these true-to-history men struggling to find their path and purpose under the leash of fate, nor how cleverly their personalities are revealed through both amusing and heartbreaking interactions between such diverse and fun characters.

 However—I’m speaking of the original content. The new scenes, translation, and romance, dispersed throughout every route in this new version, in fact ruined the whole thing for me. If I hadn’t played the original and didn’t know about the gem hidden underneath all the new garbage, I certainly would have given this a negative rating. If you want to hear me rant about the horribly written new content, feel free to read the second half of this review in Edo Blossoms. But I can’t quite bring myself to betray a story I loved for so many years.

From the beginning, there has been plenty of criticism for the protagonist, and in part I support that criticism: she’s passive, inept, dumb as a doorknob, and is pretty much good at only two things: preparing tea and cleaning. -.- (Not true: she can also cook, sew, and kiss your booboos better.) However! Remember the time period: there weren’t too many girls running around town with swords, or who were allowed to be particularly assertive (especially when surrounded by the absurdly forceful and violent Shinsengumi warriors—warriors, not a host club). But, to be honest, I found that somewhat refreshing. In a gaming world where protagonist females have to be butt-kicking, male-dominating, ego-wielding combatants, it was nice to be reminded that women can have multiple qualities that have nothing to do with killing people. And Yukimura, the protagonist, has many—and they happen to be things that girls (or anyone) could actually emulate in a normal world and still have friends. So I like her, even if she is a dimwit. But she grows (by Edo Blossoms), like any good character should. And eventually they will stop telling you to go bed on time. 

If you really want to be concerned about something, you’d be better off worrying why there’s an entire game dedicated to a defenseless girl attracted to the bestial side of men who, pitying their carnal lack of self-control, enables them to hurt and use her. But eh. 

Truthfully, after the ‘now with added romance’ aspect of the expansion, I’m reluctant to recommend the game at all. The new ‘romance’ is way too heavy, and the smutty descriptions they use are uncomfortable, ill-fitting, and laughably silly most of the time. The transition into them is equally jarring, as though they called in a special harlequin translator just for those scenes with no regard for the theme or characters. Really, the best word I can use to describe it is stomach-turning. If this is a concern for you, there’s always the option of playing an older version where the romance is far more innocent and sweet.

I’m not a huge fan of the supernatural aspect of the game either (or Kaoru’s nonsensical whining)—the story really didn’t need it. And I really don’t want to see men licking blood from veins. But some people like that it seems. Maybe you do. Maybe you don’t. Fair warning.

The crown jewel of the game, however, is the history. Oh the people who wrote this game loved their history! And because of them, I love this history now too. The Shinsengumi were remarkable men with remarkable stories, and in this game you will hear them all and live in the emotion of it and experience the confusion of a nation-changing era. I appreciated too that, though this is an otome, there is still so much sword fighting and discussion about warriors!—like the writers knew that us ladies like to see some martial action too, and want to know what it feels like to be in the middle of a battle. But there is also a very respectful treatment of what it must feel like to be a soldier, in their successes and loses and confusion over right and wrong. I don’t typically see that in a made-for-men war story, so this one feels somehow more honest, and you can see the hearts of men exposed in ways I think they would not be so willing to show to their comrades, but only to a woman like our protagonist.

I really don’t recommend planning on playing [i]all[/i] the routes (unless you really want the achievements) because by bachelor number 12, you’re going to get pretty sick of ground kicking, screaming furies, tumbling down the same ex machina hill over and over, and Amagiri’s patronizing interruptions. But I can guarantee that it’s going to be hard to choose just one route, so you can anticipate putting in at least 20 hours per game (50+ if you want the achievements).

In deciding your new romantic pursuit, I’d suggest just playing the game and following around whoever looks most interesting, but I also suggest starting with one of the original characters because their routes are lightyears better than the new content.  The following link is a preview of those original characters plus a review of the still interesting but poorly presented routes from the new content: [url=https://steamcommunity.com/app/589530/discussions/0/1742220359690125284/]Individual Character Review[/url].

 So here’s the real question. Should you save 60$ dollars (hopefully less on a good sale) and just watch the anime? Yeah, probably. However, if you really want to admire these men and find out their whole story and all their personal struggles, then you’ll need to play the game. You’ll get a peek in the anime, and the pacing’s definitely better, but you really only get to follow one man’s story. Also, you will cry. But you will cry more if you play the game first. Then, after you’ve done both, and you need to stop crying, watch the movie because it’s beautiful, high quality, and the music still makes my heart seize up when I listen to it. If you’re not into the romance (or creepy blood-letting), and would prefer the PG version, the anime is likely the best version of them all.

I want to preface this review by saying that I was familiar with the Shinsengumi and their role as cultural icons in Japanese media and extended culture as a whole, even before playing this game. Perhaps no other Japanese political group has been romanticized as much as they have, it is quite fascinating to me. The end of the Bakumatsu period signaled a big shift for Japan, after all. This game is a testament to all those ideas, attributes, and even exaggerations bestowed upon the group and their history together. Of course, you don't have to know about the Shinsengumi beforehand to enjoy this game. It does a good job at explaining the era's political climate, and the glossary feature is helpful if you want to learn more as well.

You should know that there is a fantasy element to the game too. It personally is what kept me so interested and wanting to come back for more each time, along with the political themes in some of the routes. It is also what sets it apart from other retellings of the history of the Shinsengumi. Each route has differences that make you want to keep playing through them and seeing how the story develops. I will say though, some are better written than others. I do not know if it is something to do with the localization, but the dialogue in certain routes did make me roll my eyes on a few ocassions. Still, each route has something that everyone can enjoy. 
Also, as other people have mentioned this particular Hakuoki game isn't as heavy on the romance as the next one (Edo Blossoms). There is ocassional romantic dialogue, but it is not the main focus.

All in all, there is a reason for why Hakuoki is one of the most popular otome franchises of them all. Kyoto Winds has a beautiful, emotional soundtrack, pretty illustrations, stellar voice acting, and a engaging rethreading of the narrative surrounding the Shinsengumi.
