Okay, so I always knew about Hakuoki. I played bits and pieces when it had been available on the Apple store for maybe $4.99 a chapter. Expensive, yes, but this game is every bit as good as people say, and dare me to be devil's advocate, but it might be even [i] better [//i].

Kyoto Winds is the first installment, and basically serves as the foundation for Edo Blossoms. This one focuses more on plot and less on romance, but...

The main complaint is the lack of romance in Kyoto Winds. Well, first, check the Game Settings and see if the Romance option is checked. Now with that out of the way, I'm going to say it. [b]Kyoto Winds is romantic [/b]. Dang it, it is! I've played about half the routes in story order so far, and needless to say, I'm impressed. I don't know why people don't think it's got romance. Sure, it's not heart-stopping proclamations of undying passion, but this too is romance. This half of Hakuoki is the very foundation of romance. The mc is able to build her trust and rapport with the men of Hakuoki. Not only that, she gets insight into their motivations and deepest insecurities. Sure, they might [i] say [/i] they're friends, but really check your interactions with real men. Compare to these men, and I dare you to say there is no romance. They trust, rely, and pay you extra heed. Count how many times they risk their lives for the mc and rethink their core values just because they place such a weight on her opinion. Not only that, but they eventually trust mc with their lives, just as if she fought along side them. Mc fought with the men where their comrades couldn't, she needed to be protected and they needed something to protect. I know that's not too popular for the modern, self-respecting woman, but it has it's own merit. I'm speaking strictly for the Shinsengumi right now, but I doubt the rest of the routes will steer too far from this. These men aren't forthcoming in this half, but come on, it's still romance. It's shy, blossoming, and unsure of itself, but damn it, it's just as beautiful as the other type, the type you play Edo Blossoms for.

As for the second gripe, the useless mc... Well, she's useful in the plot, and she does get some things done, though they seem insignificant. I think this is remedied with a deeper understanding of society during this time period. Mc is a woman with minimal skill in the midst of the most talented and strong men in all of Japan. Of course, she's useless. If [spoiler] furies [/spoiler] can be killed with two swings of a talented sword, then she could definitely be killed with four. Give her some slack, guys. Her uselessness was hard to watch sometimes, or most of the times, but realistically, she was better off surviving useless than dying early being mildly useful. Sure, I do wish she trained and made use of [spoiler] her demon blood [/spoiler], but I'm going to tentatively say that making her resolve epic fights with stroke-of-luck and the barest skill would have been a little... cheaty. She's got limited sword skill, weak physique, and average intelligence. [spoiler] The fact that she's a demon seems irrelevant to her potential, as she seems to have none of that demonic strength and speed the others do. I'm inclined to believe those traits are reserved to the male demons, correct me if I'm wrong. Sen did not seem strong either. [/spoiler]

If you're looking at this wondering if you should buy the game, or maybe you're considering skipping this one and only getting Edo Blossoms, GET KYOTO WINDS. I'm not a person who is a long time fan of this, in fact I hardly knew much til now. But I know that you'd be doing yourself a huge disservice not getting both parts of Hakuoki as they are equally important. Buy it bundled if you can, just get your grubby hands on this game. You won't regret it.

I'll keep this as short as possible;

One of my favourite anime show is Rurouni Kenshin (or Samurai X as I've learned what it's called in the west). For some reason I kept thinking about the show frequently while I was playing the game. The era which the game takes place, music, story,...basically everything was perfect in my opinion. I guess it gave me similar vibes?

The game is amazingly as historically accurate as it can be. Well, obviously it is not but you learn a lot about the last years of Edo/Tokugawa period and how Meiji Period came to the scene. Information regarding to the historical figures (all of the LI's basically) are also accurate -of course not regarding the ones related to the story. 

You have 12 LI's to choose from. While the prologue of the story is the same for every route, every LI's story is remarkably different from the other. There is a main story going on and it too is mainly the same but it goes a bit differently in each route. It's like LI's are the different players in this story and you see the big picture from their and MC's perspective. The main event is there and you play a different role and although some things change, main thing doesn't. (Yeah, it may not make much sense but I don't know how to explain it better) 

Don't expect heavy & steamy love scenes. The romance is quite light all over. It is not a bad thing though, in fact, it was quite refreshing to play a game where everyone doesn't try to get into each others pants.

Each route has a good, bad and unrequited love ending. Also each chapter before the last one has an ending which is "game over" You have to see ALL to unlock all achievements so check how to "skip read" lol. 

The MC is the one of best among the otome games I've played. She is not a total pushover or naive girl you usually see in these type of games. She is not very strong (the reason is explained a bit in Edo Blossoms) or particularly clever but she is not annoyingly dumb which is a huge plus for me. She doesn't fall for the LI's because "they made her heart flutter with the smoulder" You can relate to her a bit at least. 

CG's, character designs and soundtrack are very good. 

Additional info: There are several Hakuoki anime shows & movies. I haven't watched them so I cannot sat which order you should watch or which one to watch. But one thing I know is that Hijikata Toshiro is the canon LI in those. It kind of makes sense even in the games when you think about it.

To sum up; probably the best otome I've ever played to this date (if I said "the best" for another, well it has been replaced with Hakuoki series) If you like otome games, this one and Edo Blossoms is definitely a "must play" for you.

[i]Hakuoki: Kyoto Winds[/i] is the companion to [i]Hakuoki: Edo Blossoms,[/i] meaning you won't enjoy the full narrative unless you play both. However, this review pertains solely to [i]Kyoto Winds.[/i]

We follow 16-yr.-old Chizuru Yukimura over a 4-year period, as she searches for her father, discovers dark secrets, and follows the famed Shinsengumi in their fight for the shogun during the very politically-unstable tail end of Japan’s Edo period.

This game is creative historical nonfiction, and while it does advertise itself as a romance game, I would say that historical drama takes precedence as a genre. Some reviewers have pointed to this as a negative for them (mostly because of false advertising), but I thought that it was more realistic. After all, Chizuru is extremely naïve and young, making certain power dynamics even more unbalanced. Until an official declaration, Japan is also constantly on the brink of civil war. The Shinsengumi are, of course, at the forefront. A full-out romance just doesn’t seem appropriate.

This is not to say that there isn’t romance [i]at all.[/i] At least, not a cheesy, in-your-face kind of ‘I love you.’ It’s a slow burn that continues post-game. One pursues twelve men, and the level of romance differs. Either way, I never felt disappointed by any of the routes (though some were more boring than others). The variety in routes was also surprising, and why one inevitably dedicates 70+ hrs. to the game. Among otome games, Hakuoki’s hailed as a classic, and this reboot did not disappoint me.

[list]
   [*]Art: great, anatomically correct art by Kazuki Yone. However, I do think that some hands are a little too big (Maybe that’s why Chizuru thinks Souji is “really good with [his] hands”?) and that Chizuru has weird head shapes and obnoxiously big eyes sometimes. These are very minor critiques, since each character has numerous beautiful CGs to collect, and each piece is done with expert use of light/shadow, color, positioning, etc. The scenery portraits are also very beautiful. It’s clear that the art was done with care.

   [*]BGM/Sound: also great, and relevant to a scene’s mood. I do not like the weird, bone cracking noise though; it sounds fake and awkward.

   [*]Vocals: I’ve read some people say that certain voices were awkwardly low and forced, but I disagree. I think that the VAs do a great job showing emotion and reflecting their characters’ personalities through their voice acting. Note: you can turn off the vocals in the settings, if you prefer.

   [*]Encyclopedia: as an American with no knowledge of Japanese history, the encyclopedia was very helpful. I appreciate the fact that it is accessible while playing and from the title screen, since some text boxes have multiple entries. I did need to consult Wikipedia multiple times, so if you’re an ignorant American like me, you might have to as well.

   [*]Story writing: considering there are twelve different men to romance (plus the normal route, if you want to count it) on top of the Shinsengumi’s history, I think that the writers did a really good job. Personally, I did not care for the supernatural part (I actually forgot that demons and Furies were a thing at times), but it never detracted from the story. In fact, the Water of Life helps to expose quite a few characters’ beliefs and moral obligations. 

I also appreciate the writers’ endeavor to showcase different perspectives through Heisuke and Ryouma, two different routes that I liked quite a bit more than others’. On the topic of Ryouma though, I have zero idea why/how he fell for Chizuru, which was confusing. Other characters’ personalities did not make a possible romance believable to me at all, which I thought was disappointing.

   [*]Heroine: personally, I don’t like Chizuru very much. Like most otome game heroines, she’s a Mary Sue, but one that I found more annoying than usual. She is frustratingly naïve and useless, and detracts from some of the other characters. She never expresses a single opinion and is constantly in need of rescue, even though she has four years for character development. Ages 16-20 are [i]prime[/i] for character development! Plus, she trains with Kondou at one point and has her kodachi at all times, but immediately gets kicked to the ground every time she raises her sword. I get it; she’s a small girl against strong, talented swordsmen (and demons), but she is a doctor’s daughter. How is it that all she can seemingly do is disinfect and bandage wounds? I think that making her knowledgeable about medicine could have remedied many of her faults. 

I know that, as a heroine, she’s supposed to be as blank as possible so that we can project ourselves onto her, but she never does a single notable thing. She makes tea and does laundry. Also, if her speech box isn’t a repetition of what someone else says (but formed as a question), it’s some stuttered, ellipses-filled variation of “What…?” or “Huh?” or “Um…not what I meant, but…,” so why does she even say anything at all? At one point, a character says something akin to: “So?! X killed Y, so why can’t I kill X?!” and Chizuru literally says, “Well…” and then gets steamrolled by the original speaker. What was the point of her opening her mouth?! 

Her blind optimism is ridiculous too; I couldn’t understand why her half-baked advice/consolations would raise romance with the guys at times. As a result, some of the routes did not seem realistic. Hajime Saito’s and Souji Okita’s come to mind; their personalities (or, Chizuru’s lack thereof, rather) made me prefer their Bad/Unrequited endings instead. Souji, in particular, is just too dominant for someone who believes that "as long as we have faith in our hearts, everything will be okay!" and doesn't even consider that, wow, we're in a war and, uh, maybe that's not true.

   [*]Translation: good, with minor complications. Granted, I do not know any Japanese, so I can’t know [i]for sure,[/i] but sometimes characters speak more than what seems to be in the text boxes. Also, the language is awkward and/or out-of-the-right-century. Typos and incorrect words are also present at times. I have no idea what IF’s editing process was like, how the translators/editors were compensated, or even how much time the translation process received, but I do recommend another round of edits. Despite this, the English translation made sense and allowed me to follow the story without issue.

   [*]UI/Button Config.: this is a port from the PS Vita, so maybe this criticism is moot. I have no idea if it’s possible to change, but while playing, one still sees the “Press X button” prompt to go to the next text box. Also, the quick save data would randomly pop up while I was reading, which was very annoying. The one time I accidentally clicked “Yes,” I was moved backward in the story. The skipping ability works great though. I also appreciate the fact that one can access any point of the narrative, with a chosen character’s route on HIGH or LOW romance (after achieving their Good Ending, that is), directly from the title screen. It makes the game much more enjoyable.
[/list]

[i]Hakuoki: Kyoto Winds[/i] is not infallible, but it is enjoyable. I definitely recommend it, and suggest that you keep in mind that the story is not over while you play it.

I've finished what's considered the "default route", and if I had to describe it in 2 words, it'd be "painfully mediocre". Which is regretful, as the game seemingly has a great setup: a young woman ends up among the samurai forces. There's so much the writers could have done with this... but unfortunately for the heroine, this is a typical Japanese visual novel, so she will spend 4 years cooking and cleaning, only have one day of sword training and call it a day, but nevertheless whine about not being included in armed conflicts and being useless overall.

At first, I thought that maybe this game was intended for Japanese history nerds, but nope. Most of the major historical events only get mentioned in passing, and what you witness instead is lots of petty squabbles with other samurai and boring slice-of-life days. Many characters purposefully keep themselves distant from the heroine (can't blame them, she's annoying), and, in the traditional spirit of Japanese games, she's expected to take their threats and verbal abuse as a wall she's supposed to break through in order to win their affection. Remember that time you were treated like trash and thought "aww, he's only doing it because he doesn't want to show how much he secretly cares about me"? Yeah, me neither. Recommended for people prone to Stockholm syndrome and/or tragically low self-esteem.

P.S. As other reviewers have noted, this is only half of the game disguised as a standalone, so it ends abruptly and on a cliffhanger.

I've never left a negative review of an otome game like this, and I didn't think I'd advise against Hakuouki in my entire life, but here goes.

They censored Kimigiku's status as an oiran -- a courtesan -- to a "geigi", or geisha. The translation has been changed in certain spots and is much poorer, with a typo right in the first few minutes of the game.

Chizuru seems dumbed down, screaming things in all-caps, and even more timid than before. This is partially to blame because the game has been lengthened. In some cases the extra scenes are welcome, in others it feels like pointless padding to make the game longer. But the more she talks, she gets more indecisive and it gets boring.

They added plenty of scenes that made it drag and drag unnecessarily. But, then, bafflingly, they cut and altered certain scenes. Scenes such as when Nagakura and Harada are speaking of the coming war -- changing this in favor of Chizuru doing silent expo-speak.

The new music is awful, and is way too modern in certain places. The battle music is a form of techno, for god's sake. It's 1864!

I think it's part of a plan to "youth up" the game. The achievements for this game are impossibly annoying -- memes and slang like "New guy, who dis?" and "Still a better love story than". That and the techno REALLY make me think that they're trying to sell this to a younger crowd.

But Hakuouki has always been timeless, and if someone is too immature that they can't play a game without sharp, techno battle music and have the characters using more slang -- Harada says "like" as in, like, the way I just used it -- then they shouldn't be playing Hakuouki in the first place.

And the new characters are boring, droll and take up too much time. I kept skipping through their parts.

The only GOOD thing is that there are more scenes with the original characters -- the five main Shinsengumi and Kazama -- and you can now romance the other 3 Shinsengumi characters: Sanan, Yamazaki and Nagakura.


One more thing? Kyoto Winds + Edo Blossoms are one whole game if you purchase the 3DS, PSP or PS3 version. So you're not shelling out tons of money for what is supposed to be one entire game.

Let me preface this by saying that you should fully understand that this is only half of the game. If you're looking to romance handsome anime guys, this is not the half of the game you're looking for, and you should know that. This is the first half, containing your friendship and history with the characters featured, and not your romance. That part of the game is called Edo Blossoms, and it is also available for download, so if you're only interested in that bit, do not purchase Kyoto Winds and get disappointed. 

As for this game, which is all of the history and buildup, it wasn't completely unenjoyable. The atmosphere and art were very nice, and the music was peaceful. It succeeds in crafting a very beautiful world and there is actually a sense of danger and consequence. 

However, I just do not like the main character. My reasons for WHY contains spoilers, so read at your own risk: 
The MC [spoiler]is a demon, and her wounds heal.[/spoiler] She is not ignorant of this, and knows she has this ability, but [spoiler]still panics in every dangerous situation. She has a sword, and it's implied she has been trained to use it, but always completely forgets about it in every moment of combat.[/spoiler] In addition, she spends what amounts to be around five years over the course of the game with these men, and never [spoiler]furthur trains herself to fight or protect herself, despite posing as a soldier, and instead just wanders the grounds, occasionally making tea or cleaning.[/spoiler] It's frustrating to play as a character with so little personal agency or self-motivation, and other characters make some great sacrifices on her behalf. It's exceptionally annoying to watch such pyrrhic victories unfold when you could have been of help had the MC had even an ounce of independent will or strength. 

Beyond the MC, the male characters' feelings towards the player can be confusing. It may be my own sensibilities getting in the way, but I find it difficult to grow meaningful attachments and bonds towards characters that purposefully keep themselves distant and short with me. The game makes no secret that the band of characters would kill your MC if she stepped out of their rules, and they bring it up regularly, oftentimes in the middle of previously jovial conversation. It feels less like an unlikely friendship between her and the characters, and more like a slow-burn Stockholm Syndrome situation. Perhaps the game wants you to feel like you need to earn their affection? Perhaps it thinks their stoic treatment towards the player makes the characters seem cool or attractive? I'm not sure, but it's certainly not for me. If you want to communicate that a feeling of trust and affection is being built between characters that were previously at odds, maybe don't continuously remind the player that you could attack them at any moment and that their wants and will do not matter. 

Maybe this is a problem I have with some otome games in general, but I do not find captor/captive situations romantic, nor do I enjoy being a damsel in distress. Maybe it's a cultural/language barrier, and there's more nuance than I'm giving it credit--other people certainly seem to like this series, and don't find it as frustrating as myself--but if you have similar feelings towards these things, and expect more agency and empathy from your characters, then you will not enjoy this game. 

Thank you for reading my review.

I might recommend this game if it were solely a historical visual novel (but that wouldn't remove the problem of historical revisionism and romanticization) but since Hakuoki is marketed as otome game, I cannot recommend it as such. It can be easy to fall for one or more of the love interests (I surely did) but the meaninglessness of the female MC that the narrative creates by always prioritizing the love interests and the lack of care given to her by both game and love interests, Hakuoki Kyoto Winds (and Edo Blossoms) fail(s) at romance.
[hr]Kyoto Winds is the first part of this edition of the Hakuoki franchise. The split into two is justified by the change in tone and game mechanics but even being half the full game's length, KW is still too long - mostly due to the abundance of love interests. Originally, the franchise had 6 love interests and while I do like two thirds of the new 6, I would have preferred it if some characters' routes were cut or the overall game were made less repetitive. This game is unplayable without a guide and if you look at one, it would seem there were many choices to make here. But when you look at their nature, you'll find that they only serve 3 functions: 1) getting MC to be in or avoid situations where she can interact with certain love interests, 2) making you choose between love interests and 3) gaining or not gaining the affection of a certain love interest. {In Edo Blossoms, the choices are only type 3) and an additional choice type which is completely redundant.} [b]If you like VNs where your choices matter (e.g. Amnesia: Memories, Heart Fragment), Hakuoki KW and EB are not for you.[/b] Another thing are the endings which, apart from the good endings, are mostly redundant and insignificant. The bad endings all end in either the MC or the love interest (LI) or both dying, whereas the unrequited love endings are either "LI leaves MC behind" or "LI sacrifices himself". [b]If you like VNs where each ending, good or otherwise, adds something to the game (experience) (e.g. Amnesia: Memories, Heart Fragment), Kyoto Winds isn't for you. [/b] {A similar thing can be said about Edo Blossoms where they added Game Over endings but those are just premature bad endings.} [/hr]
[hr]Aesthetically at least, this game does not disappoint. The art and CGs are great, the music is solid but can get on your nerves if you play through the whole game.[/hr]
[hr]Overall, if you're interested in this game, just watch playthroughs of it online. Neither KW nor EB are games that need to be played since they are linearly structured and probably the most literal definition of "visual novel" - a novel with visuals. And Hakuoki doesn't need your money, it's getting enough at home because everything Shinsengumi-related is highly popular in Japan (thanks to the romanticization of the past and yearning for a time where samurai still existed and were fighting against change).[/hr]
[hr]CWs (that I noticed): Mild depiction of blood, textual descriptions of violence and gore, use of alcohol and inebriation (by/of the love interests), verbal abuse & control of the MC (by love interests and others), sexism and conservative gender roles e.g. towards the MC (by love interests and others), familial mistreatment of the MC (by sibling and parent).[/hr]

I've been a big fan of Hakuouki since the PSP version came out and I was really looking forward to playing it with all the promised new content. But as much as I love it, I can't recommend this version for multiple reasons.

First: This is not the whole game; it is roughly two thirds of the story and the part that was called the 'common route' in the original game. And it ends when any romance option you may have achieved with your decisions just starts to bloom. Since Edo Blossoms is out already, you can continue on the spot, but you are forced to buy a second game to get the whole story.

Second: It is not a romantic story. As mentioned above, this game covers the ‘common route’ and that means you only get a glimpse of budding romance right before it ends. As it is set in a time when Japan renewed itself in a bloody civil war, there are many dark aspects you will discover. And as if the times weren’t grim enough then, the game adds even more dark stuff to that, so if you are unlucky with your decisions, you can have a very dark, very depressing experience. Also, the game wants to tell the story of the Shinsengumi and their fight in those stormy times, so prepare for a long history lesson. I loved it, but I’m a history geek and quite in love with the past of Japan. I just wanted to warn you in case this is not your cup of tea.

Third: The translation. Oh God, the translation… I know that not everyone knows Japanese and would (or would want to) notice this, but I’m already at the point where it really hurts reading the subtitles. And my Japanese isn’t all that good, so I’m sure there is even more than what I've spotted so far. It’s not only that the men ‘sound’ so much more aggressive and ill-willed in the text and that it often doesn’t fit with how they talk in Japanese. I understand that this may be due to localizing the game for a Western audience. But there are translation mistakes even in really short, easy sentences where the meaning is completely garbled and even some instances where it felt like they had given up on translating altogether and just invented some stuff that seemed fitting for the scene. And even the English sentences often have grammar mistakes that forced me to interpret more than read. I expect more from a VN of this caliber, especially for this price.

And last: Neither the developer nor the publisher seems to have any interest in their game here on Steam apart from how much money it makes them. There are some issues with the performance of the game that are still unaddressed. I didn’t have any issues except for the small bug that the characters don’t say my heroine’s name when using the default ‘Chizuru’. But even that is still open, no response from anyone working on the game as far as I could see in the discussions.

So, even though I love Hakuouki, I can sadly only tell you this: If you are one of the few people who own a PSP, try to find the original game. The translation of that was not perfect either, maybe it wasn’t even good, but sadly it was still better than what we get here. And I still prefer the art of the original game, especially with regard to the uniforms. It was gorgeous. To be fair the art in this new version of the game is one of the few good points it has. It still looks beautiful. But that is not enough, so I have to give this a thumbs down. I’m so sad right now…

Kyoto Winds cosplays as a suspenseful mystery, light-hearted comedy, action movie, and an easy-going novel. All the grim and gloomy is painted over with frivolousness and suffocatingly heteronormative romance. One must be a bat short of a belfry to romanticise their own jailers and ruthless murderers willing to massacre an innocent child.

Hakuoki’s writing is the pinnacle of generic. Its story opens with a recycled premise: the protagonist is taken hostage and her fate is decided by a mysterious cabal. Narration is jarringly motley as it juxtaposes rudimentary English with conspicuously advanced vocabulary. The simplicity of language is further contrasted by ponderous sentence construction. This makes it impossible to perceive the characters as humans instead of caricatures playing at one. Common leaps in judgment and confusing non sequiturs render the experience even less believable.

If I close both my eyes and pretend to overlook thirst traps with no follow-up and insultingly strict gender stereotypes, Hakuoki has a few saving graces, rescuing it from entering textbooks as a bottom-of-the-barrel otome schlock. For instance, soundtrack is unique, euphoric and vivifies the game. 

The backgrounds and clothing are drawn with skill – they paint the picture of places where events take place vividly. The would-be ikemen faces, however, taint the aesthetics terribly.

2/10

After playing for hours to finish both parts, what was I rewarded with? An awful, awful ending of an awfully outdrawn, tragic and depressing story. I mean, who came up with the idea of making an otome-game set in the paradigm shift between the Shoguns and Samurai and the rapid implementation of modern Western-warfare? War is depressing enough; war between an underwhelmingly small force armed with sticks and swords and an overwhelmingly large army armed with the time's most advanced and modern weaponry - that's just cruel and brutal. So if that's what they were going for, they did a really good job at making you feel inferior, constantly, and hopeless. Yes, the devs made an otome game into a horrific take on micro skirmishes, which are undoubtedly the most brutal occurances in war, and they made your character - and the guy you like - a part of it.

Going into the game, I expected there to be charming Samurai and perhaps a touch of the occult, seeing as some of the screenshots of part 2 depicts vampire-esque behavior. I expected there to be a lot of characters and a compelling story for each of them with plenty of ups and downs - with at least one happy ending for each of them. I didn't demand more, just one good ending to satisfy my vicarious, "guilty pleasure"-urge. However, for the guy I chose, there wasn't, and all throughout the playthrough, people died left to right, both major and minor characters. Sometimes, they just were killed, while sometimes, they commited "honorable suicide". Every time, there was nothing but a passing mention of it, with no impact on the "chosen" storyline or your character.

Also, the female MC. She was awful. Awful! Personality like your frugal grandma's sixty-year-old dishrag and with as much activity in her brain as a goldfish with an extra chromosome or two. She was unbearably frustrating, like a young cousin you're tasked to take care of during a family gathering just because she's a young and cute and adorable. I seriously wanted to grab her and shake her to see if at least coins would fall out of her ears. Alas, I couldn't, but if this crap was in VR, you know I'd grab a baseball bat and smack myself until I, too, became as vapid and insipid as her, if only to escape her painfully suffocating wallflower personality. Fortunately and unfortunately, she didn't have very much to say, but practically just stood there, watching the men, being "supportive" and "down-to-earth" and "lovable" at times. *shudder*

The "bachelors" are the best thing about the game, as should be. The voice actors are top-notch, and some of them really carry the overall performance, eliciting emotion within me. But they're not nearly given enough screen time, and the choices you have to pick to win their favor is incredibly--no, ridiculously vague. I'm serious, the choices you must make to increase your relationship with a certain guy are so random and bland: a good example is when you have to choose between either seeking out the men, fleeing on your own or staying where you are. Now, do any of these choices say anything at all about the man they're connected to? No! This game must be either savescummed or played with a walkthrough - there is no intuitiveness or clever game design where you can sort of figure out what guy would prefer a certain choice. I'd recommend looking up a guide and having it right next to you, or else it will take you more than double the time to finish the game, and most likely, you will have ended up on the completely wrong dude's path. 

What with 12 guys to choose from, there are just way too many characters. Side characters and antagonists that just appear for a single or a few scenes - only to disappear and never be heard from or mentioned again. I get that the devs want you to replay the game through its many endings and character paths on where you can meet and learn more about these random people, but the romance is just not good enough for that dedication to be warranted. And though the devs managed to build quite a cast and a sort of emotional resonance with some of the guys in which their personalities really showed, they throw all of it away in plot turns from hell and abrupt character death. It's like GoT before the scriptwriters decided fanservice was more important than a compelling and unique story.

Although the writing is rather average in both a good and bad way, there were a few times when I laughed or reacted in a "nice one" or "ahaaa!" way. Though, that might have just been because my brain was putrefying under the duress of roleplaying our female MC's astronomical IQ level. You won't find any gems here, and the translation quality varies at times. Knowing a bit of Japanese myself, there are discrepancies at times. None too damaging, except for one that practically ruined the "sweet tender confession moment" at the end of the storyline since he already had told this empy coconut-head of an MC that he loved her. There's also this weird dissonance between the time that passes in these transition slides and what the MC narrates. It won't be game-breaking, but it will be frustrating and break immersion.

And now, the story. The guy I chose was the gorgeous, hard-shelled and relenteless leader of the merry band of wannabe-samurai. I just can't resist guys like that, and I don't think any female really can (though I will say, he got uncomfortably verbally abusive at times). The story was alright during the first game: there was mystery, intrigue, several factions that plotted against each other, all against this historical backdrop - with a hint of the occult. Not only was the story in the second part incredibly boring, drawn-out and uninteractive, I didn't at all feel connected to the guy until the very last day - to only have that happiness (or at least satisfaction, because trust me, I wasn't at all happy when the two characters got together after excrutiating hours of conversations about war and politics with names you forget as soon as they mention them) ripped away. You also feel just like an observer most of the time, with no proactiveness of your own, and your character barely reacts when they finally find their missing father, whom they have been searching for for years.

This is a visual novel, yes, and technically an otome with surprisingly much blood and swearing. However, if you're looking for that rush in your system when the two main characters interact, and the gradual climax of a relationship, you're looking at the wrong game. I bought both games for 6 euro, so it wasn't that damaging, especially since the voice acting, again, is nothing short of incredible. And there's this fun silly atmosphere with an accompaning banter that you can expect from this tight-knitted group of samurai/childhood friends, which you can bask in at rare occasions. So if you've got the money and time, and this thing is on at least 85% sale, sure, go for it. Enjoy. But do not expect to indulge.

Play Cinderella Phenomenon or Amnesia: Memories instead. The first one is free and the second one is half the price of this first part. And though Amnesia: Memories is nowhere as complex in terms of worldbuilding as this game, it excels at romance and chemistry between you (the player), the MC and the male interest - which is what otome games should do.

Let's get the good stuff out of the way first, because in many ways the game is very GOOD:

High quality art, variety of music, beautiful backgrounds and characters, well-written story with multiple branches, dedication to historial accuracy while not getting lost in boring details, good translation quality and voice acting, perfect game menu and shortcuts (including the usual Skip Read, Quick Save, Encyclopedia, Jump to Chapter, Gallery, etc.)

The keyboard controls could be a little better, as sometimes they don't work how you'd expect in special circumstances. 

Here's why the game gets a negative recommendation from me:

IT IS TOO DEPRESSING TO PLAY.

The guy you choose gets injured.  The guys you don't choose get injured or die.  The NPCs die.  You get hurt and die (sometimes).  Everything is a bloody mess.  I know, it's this way because it's basically civil war in Japan (Boshin War) and you're hanging with the Shinsegumi (who lose the war), but most people play romance games to have a good time.  If you're looking for a good time and don't want to see hot guys cut up and killed all day, pick another game.

TL;DR: THIS IS WORTH PLAYING IF YOU LIKE OTOME GAMES. It is professionally made with well produced music and pretty art. Personally this isn't worth the normal price though! Wait for a sale! (I got both for like 10 bucks I think).

Review: This is a review of boths games. I do this because, as many have expressed here: this is just the first half of the game and it is not (in my opinion) enjoyable without the companion game Edo Blossoms, which gives the actual ending. You should know what you're getting into before you spend the default price.

Why the thumbs down? Because this is NOT a feel good, nor particularly romantic game. I play otome games for the romance man. Heated moments of passion and nice writing. Preferably with a true happy ending. I could deal with tragedy if the romance was super developed... WHICH  IT ISN'T HERE. Not to say there isn't romance at all, but rather the romance that exists is sparse as hell and doesn't affect the direction of events. 

The story, namely the basic historical events of the fall of the Shogun, is what takes front here. Which again would be fine if the story was... GOOD. But it really isn't. Its obvious that the fantasy part was just shoved in there to make it something other than pure historical fiction and is thusly not so well developed. There are so many ways they could have given the player more control or added more tension to the romance. But they didn't. every single thing that happens in this game is anti-climactic.

And if you're waiting for good romance moments in the second... Don't get your hopes up. Reviews here made is sound like this was build up and the next one was full of romance (I love slow burns!) so I was excited.

I was horribly disappointed. I get the impression that the happy endings were meant to be bitter sweet, but it severely lacked on the sweetness part. Like eating a lemon rind when you thought you were getting lemonade.

A lot of this game was boring. A lot of the big events in history were text dumped on you. It's so boring it was hard to sit through the text dumps so I'd walk away and forget it was on (which  is why the play time is so long!) It was a struggle to get through without yawning. This game is older now and pretty much seemed to set off the shit ton of otome Shinsegumi games, so props for that BUUUT.... Let me tell you: THERE ARE MUCH BETTER SHINSENGUMI GAMES. Voltage has one that really tugged my heart strings and did it without some stupid poorly developed fantasy sub plot. And with a reasonably useful lead character, I might add.

So buy it, on sale. If you're bored.
